items.title: 'I just have to reiterate the power that we have as riders' - Lombardia protest ringleader Ben Healy emboldened as he calls for change on rider safety
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
The five minute delay before the start of Il Lombardia at the close of the European season demonstrated the power riders have in forcing better safety in races, according to Ben Healy (EF Education-EasyPost).

Rider safety has been the hottest topic in road cycling since the terrible death of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal in the summer. And when that incident was followed by a series of further near-misses during the Italian autumn Classics, something had to give.

Healy was the driving force behind what he calls a 'stand' rather than a protest, the peloton delaying the start of Il Lombardia, the season’s final Monument, by five minutes. But, as powerful as the delay was, and as hard hitting and articulate as Remco Evenepoel’s (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) words were, the demonstration was an example of the power riders have.

"I think we just really wanted to show as riders the power that we had, and that we're not happy," he told in a café close to the bustle of the Rouleur Live show, where he was fulfilling sponsor commitments.

"We didn't want to just go at the Lombardia organisers, for instance. You know that's why we chose to do a five-minute stand before the race actually started, and just delay the race, and just show that if this continues, that this is what we can do if we choose to."

"I think after that happened [with Tarling] everyone expected something to change, you know, and when we went to Italy, there were what, three cars on the course in separate races over three or four days? And that was pretty clear then that nothing had changed," Healy said.

"There has to be a process to make things safer. And I mean, for sure, the UCI is aware of it, but I don't know how aware they are, they’re not on the ground every single race. This is clearly something that is recurring, and it just shouldn't happen ever, having a car on the course, let's just hope the UCI will listen and work with us to make change."

If Lombardia was the example of what unity within the peloton can do in bringing an issue to notice, Healy prefers not to commit to what might happen if and when such a dangerous situation occurs again, or worse, should another rider die.

"I just really hope it doesn't come to that, you know? I just have to reiterate the power that we have as riders and ultimately what we can do if we choose to.

"Mistakes can be made, and as long as we're working towards making racing safer, I think that's the most important thing. We don't want to point blame or, like, kick and scream, it’s about being productive and working together to improve the sport for everyone."

items.title: Shirin van Anrooij to make cyclo-cross debut with Canyon-SRAM alongside Zoe Backstedt next week
items.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
items.content:
Shirin van Anrooij will make her debut with Canyon-SRAM in the upcoming UCI Cyclo-cross World Cup in Ostrava, Czechia, next week, racing alongside Zoe Bäckstedt at the start of a 13-race schedule, the team announced on Friday.

She has been training in Malaga, Spain alongside her new teammate and former under-23 cyclo-cross rival Bäckstedt in preparation for the intensive campaign of 11 World Cups, the National Championships and culminating with the World Championships in Oostende, Belgium in January.

"I'm just really excited and looking forward to starting the season because we've been watching CX racing on TV for a couple of weeks now, and I'm really curious to see how it is amongst the girls again," Van Anrooij said in the team press release.

"I think Zoe and I are having a good preparation camp here in Malaga, so I can't wait to be on the start line myself, and to see where my level is at."

"I'm hoping that I'll reach my best level in cyclo-cross again, and then I'll just have to discover what results this will bring me," Van Anrooij said.

"I think the biggest goals are, for sure, the Christmas period with a lot of races that I really like – Koksijde, Zonhoven, Gavere, and then the World Championships in Oostende. Worlds is always a big goal for everyone, but I especially look forward to that, with it being a race on the sand in Belgium."

After her first year racing in the elite fields last season, with nine races from the end of December through Worlds, Bäckstedt is looking forward to a longer campaign. "I'm really excited for this cyclo-cross season. It feels like it's been two years since I properly raced CX as last year was an extremely short season for me.

"It's super fun having Shirin as my teammate. Already for training, it's been really beneficial for me to follow her and learn from her. I'm now excited to do our first race together."

Although both riders have goals for the early part of the 2027 road season, Canyon-SRAM's performance director Dan Fleeman supports their off-road ambitions.

"I think cyclo-cross offers several important benefits. From a physical perspective, it develops the ability to repeatedly produce high-intensity efforts, accelerate out of corners, change pace and deal with constantly changing demands. It also requires a high level of anaerobic capacity and the ability to recover quickly between efforts.

"Technically, the benefits are equally important. CX develops bike handling, balance, coordination and the ability to make decisions under pressure. Riders are constantly adapting to different terrain and conditions, managing their effort and finding the quickest way through a course.

"Also, I think that there is a mental benefit. CX is an incredibly demanding discipline where you have to be prepared to push yourself outside your comfort zone, deal with mistakes, and keep fighting throughout a race."

Their calendar has been designed to focus only on the major races, skipping the Superprestige, X2O Trofee, and HG Cross.

"The main consideration is quality over quantity. The World Cup offers the highest level of competition, the best opportunities to measure ourselves against the world's leading riders, and the experience of racing on some of the biggest stages in cyclo-cross.

"We also have to consider the overall demands of the season. Both riders have important road objectives, so we don't want to overload the programme with racing simply for the sake of racing. We would rather be selective, target the important events, and make sure that they arrive at them in good physical condition."

items.title: From plumbing to Picnic PostNL – The Dutch team's newest recruit with dreams of Amstel Gold Race and riding with Wout van Aert
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
The lowest-ranked team in the WorldTour last year, Picnic PostNL, have made plenty of changes to their roster next season, with nine new faces and counting.

Joining the Dutch team in their quest for more success in 2027 is Belgian racer Daan Depuydt, who comes on board from Continental squad Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions.

The 23-year-old, who previously raced at amateur level, enjoyed several standout rides this year, including a Tour de Limousin stage win and three top-10 finishes at the Tour de Wallonie. His rise to the WorldTour has been a rapid one, given he was working as a plumber just a few years ago.

Depuydt, who also did odd jobs as a gardener and electrician, told that, "Actually, I was never really consciously focused on landing a professional contract. I just raced because I enjoyed it."

He primarily raced on the mountain bike as a junior, picking up four Belgian titles before struggling with back injuries. On the road, he raced in Belgium with amateur squad VP Consulting before catching the eye of Baloise-Het Poetsbureau – Sven Nys' team – with a stage win at the Triptyque Ardennais in 2025.

He hit the ground running this year, with June's Tour de Wallonie only the second UCI-ranked race of his career after the Antwerp Port Epic in May.

"I was riding there with broken ribs, because I had a bad fall 2 days before the opening stage," he told . In August, there was another top ride in Limousin, where he finished second on the opening day before winning stage 3.

"After my second place in the opening stage, I wanted to win one of the remaining 3 stages at all costs. And in the third stage, I struck gold," he said.

"After the opening stage, I suddenly started receiving messages from teams. But I never thought I'd actually secure a spot – especially after reading an article about how many riders were still without a team for the season."

Soudal-QuickStep were among the teams to show interest, though they were already full for 2027. Choosing Picnic PostNL was a no-brainer, he said, despite recent reports of a 'culture of fear' at the team.

"When the moment finally came to put pen to paper with Picnic PostNL, I didn’t have to think twice. I had a good feeling right from the start of our conversations. They prioritise the riders' interests and are always open to feedback," he said.

"Sure, it’s a strict team, but name me one WorldTour team that isn't. As a team, you have expectations of your riders, and vice versa. That dynamic can – and should – be a bit strict, provided it’s handled fairly."

Depuydt sees himself as a puncheur who excels on shorter climbs while also sprinting well from a small group. He's hoping to race on his home training roads at Amstel Gold Race next season, and is dreaming of racing alongside his idol, Wout van Aert – a goal which shows just how far he's come since his plumbing days.

"I see myself as a puncheur. Short climbs suit me thanks to my past as a mountain biker. But I have also noticed this year that I am fast. I am not a pure sprinter; I am too light for that. But after a tough race, I can finish well in a reduced group," he said.

"I've never ridden a race with Wout. I would think it's really cool if that happens next year. If we stand at the start of a race together, I will look for Wout and ride behind him for a bit to take a look at him.

"If I could just follow him for a little while on a climb, that would be a huge dream come true."

items.title: WorldTour team ignored by new Collective Cycling Group reform project
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
The nascent Collective Cycling Group (CCG), a coalition of teams bidding to overhaul cycling’s economic model, did not seek the involvement of all the WorldTour teams, with Human Powered Health telling they were ignored by the project.

The CCG, which is the new version of the failed One Cycling movement, launched publicly on Wednesday, with 24 teams coming together in a bid to "unlock the value potential of professional cycling".

Not all 32 teams from across the men’s and women’s WorldTour agreed to sign up to the new company, with Tadej Pogačar’s UAE Team Emirates the most notable of the teams who have declined to be involved.

However, one WorldTour team, Human Powered Health, were not even approached.

A spokesperson for the US outfit, which has operated in the Women’s WorldTour since 2022, told that senior management were not made aware of the CCG nor of any opportunity to take part in such a project.

The complete overlooking of an established WorldTour team raises early question marks over the unity of the CCG, which was described by its CEO Oliver Ciesla as a “broad and inclusive initiative”.

Furthermore, it was not billed as a closed shop, with the announcement stating that discussions with other teams are ongoing.

The project is largely made up of WorldTour teams but two second-division men’s outfits, Pinarello-Q36.5 and Tudor Pro Cycling are shareholders in the company, too.

Contacted on Friday in relation to Human Powered Health's position, a spokesperson for the Collective Cycling Group said: "CCG has brought together a significant group of leading professional cycling teams, and we are open for that group to grow over time."

With summer behind us, thermal bib tights back in rotation, and a winter of hiding from the rain on Zwift on the horizon, that can only mean one thing: Black Friday is fast approaching.

Like mine, I expect your inbox is full of Black Friday promotions, and the latest to land in mine is a huge Black Friday Wahoo rundown; a list of everything we can expect from Wahoo Fitness, the cycling tech mainstay from Atlanta.

Wahoo's own Black Friday sale kicks off today - November 20th - with deals across smart trainers, indoor bikes and treadmills, but there are plenty of other deals if you know where to look.

So no matter if you're shopping for a new smart trainer, a bike computer, a heart rate monitor, or even a treadmill, you're in the right place to find the best price and the best advice.

If you want to take it a step further, you can add on the Zwift Ride v2 smart frame too. This still uses the Kickr Core v2, but the frame replaces your bike, saving you the need to wheel it through your house. It's also more widely adjustable, so you can share it with others in the house. View Deal

Wahoo is slowly branching out into running, and the Kickr Run is its first foray into treadmills. I've not used it, but the general consensus is that it's very good. View Deal

Whether running or cycling, if you're doing it indoors you'll want a really good fan to help keep you cool. This is still the gold standard in that space, and although the price is steep, mine is still running strong after seven years of regular use. View Deal

This is a bit of an odd one as Amazon says its retail price is 624.99. That's not true, it's actually $499.99. However, it's still a nice discount on the biggest model in Wahoo's GPS computer range. View Deal

In our opinion, it's likely the best for most people. Great navigation, great features, and very user friendly. View Deal

This one's the smallest model in the range. It's perhaps more of a racer's choice, but it also packs more or less all the features of the Roam into a smaller package.

That means it's cheaper still, but the smaller screen can be limiting in some cases. View Deal

This is the same as the product above, but with the Zwift Cog and Click add-on, which replaces the cassette with a single-speed cog that's compatible with all modern groupsets. The 'Click' then lets you shift virtually in-game, which is silent, unlike the loud clunk you sometimes get from a derailleur. View Deal

But before you commit to the V6, consider this, which is potentially better and currently the same price.

The Kickr Move uses the same internals as the current Kickr smart trainer, but adds a moveable track to allow you to roll forward and backward under high load, and a few degrees of left-right tilt too.

In use, the left-right tilt makes for a slightly unusual ride feel, since it doesn't self-centre like a bike. I often felt I was fighting it with core strength or simply sitting at an angle. View Deal

The Zwift Ride V2, paired with Kickr Core 2, is the whole-bike indoor solution, saving your own bike from the wear and tear. Its broad adjustability also means you can share it with others in your home, or try out new positions without changing the fit on your main bike.View Deal

Or a halfway house between the two, the Kickr Bike Shift, which offers the quiet operation and broad adjustability, but foregoes the tilting and a few other features to keep the price down. View Deal

Wahoo is primarily a cycling-focussed company, but it's slowly branching out into running, and this Kickr Run is its first foray into treadmills. View Deal

items.title: From aero pockets made on a dining table to skinsuits worn by Mark Cavendish – How one rider took Nopinz from Devon to a world-leading 'everyday aero' brand
items.author: Andy McGrath
items.content:
A couple of thousand years before bike racing even existed, Plato had it right: necessity is the mother of all invention.

An elite racer in the UK finishing at the sharp end of the country’s time trials on highways and byways, Blake Pond was getting into an unwanted routine. He would lovingly spend several minutes getting his race number pinned perfectly for every time trial. It was a need, driven by aesthetics, aerodynamics and fastidiousness.

When he jumped on the bike, rode off and heard a ripping noise, he knew what it meant: gigantic pinholes in a speed suit which had cost a week of his bike shop mechanic wages. The alternative fate was just as undesirable: he would pass riders with numbers flapping like parachutes. "On the drive back, I was thinking there’s got to be a better way of doing this," Pond tells over coffee.

His solution: a stretchy pocket, as you’d find on a documents-enclosed envelope, stuck on a skinsuit with special adhesive. Initially, the idea went in his training kit drawer for a few years, doubting its mass appeal. But he was drawn back to it after hearing other racers airing their frustration or even yelps of pain from competitors accidentally getting stuck by a pin-wielding friend trying to give them perfectly flat race numbers.

In 2014, Nopinz was born with the SpeedPocket. At first, it was just Pond, his computer and a heat press. The next iteration involved using a seamstress to sew in this aero addition before posting the garment back.

In little more than a decade, his company has gone from the dining room table in the Devon town of Bideford in the south-west of the United Kingdom and a self-explanatory brand name to more than 50,000 orders and the WorldTour, with a range of apparel and aerodynamic accessories tailored for TT, road racing, triathlon, running and indoor cycling. The WorldTour teams and riders supported along the way include Mark Cavendish on his record-breaking 'Project 35' stage-win quest at the Tour de France.

Nopinz wouldn't be where it is today without the community’s explosion of interest in aero gains over the last decade. "How optimised everyone’s got in TT is crazy. When I was racing back in 2014, I had a lot of watts but not a lot of aero," Pond reflects. "And now it’s shifted the other way completely. I’m going the same sort of speed as I was back then, off 15 per cent less power."

An aero obsessive, Pond climbed a lamppost at the 2015 Tour de France prologue in Utrecht to take photographs of riders from above. This obsession feeds their comprehensiveness, testing products in the wind tunnel at Silverstone, prototyping in-house and doing fabric tests.

WorldTour recognition for 'everyday aero' kit

"We always test and market the averages. If we test at 40, 45 and 50 [km/h] and nought to seven degrees of yaw, we’ll average it out across the speeds we’re aiming that product at," he says, implying that they do not cherry-pick certain data for marketing. Alongside the weighted model designed to better reflect real-world riding conditions that he mentions, theirs is a competitive price point: their popular Sonic socks cost £24.99.

Pond has tried to keep their pricing reasonable, though he is aware of the perverse "reassuringly expensive" philosophy that can pervade in the sport. More expensive does not necessarily mean better. "We need to make the margin in the suit and obviously get profit out of it, but it comes to a stage where you’re making it up, really. Sometimes that does happen with other brands – I can’t understand why the suits are so pricey when we can do it [for cheaper] and do all the R&D," he says.

For the founder, Nopinz suits are for the person who can’t spend £20,000 in a wind tunnel. "Maybe we’re doing it more cost-effectively. There’s a ceiling price: we want to be that reliable sort of partner: you know you’re getting a really good product and it’s not stupidly expensive. That’s how I see it really: NoPinz – everyday aero."

As the framed and signed jerseys around their HQ in the Devon town of Barnstaple attest, the WorldTour wanted a piece of their watt savers too. Starting with support for LottoJumbo-NL in 2015, riders from the likes of FDJ, Israel-Premier Tech and AG2R have all benefited. Alex Dowsett bought his own skinsuits from the company and wore one to win a 2020 Giro d’Italia stage.

The company became an official TT partner to WorldTour team Intermarché the next season, giving it visible "additional credibility" after years of secretly supplying ingredients to the bunch, without recognition or under an NDA.

Pond says Nopinz was offered a full clothing partnership with the Belgian squad but couldn't accommodate the approximate £500,000 outlay, nor the quantity of kit. "That sort of commitment would be crushing," he says.

Still, teams or riders came calling with projects – and you might be surprised at how disorganised and last-minute pro cycling can be. One of the company’s latest nights on the job involved working with takeaway boxes after Israel-Premier Tech realised several days before the Tour de France start that they had sent the wrong designs for their special edition skinsuits. One of their coaching team drove from the south of France to Devon, got a few hours’ kip in Pond’s campervan while Nopinz put on a production run of 50 suits, turning it around in 24 hours in time for him to drive to the Grand Départ.

Cutting-edge materials and UCI pushback

There is a knick-knack sign in Pond’s home which says 'One bike ride away from a good mood'. He was inspired to get in the saddle by hearing tales of the sport: his grandfather, Lew Pond, was a rival of British track sprint icon Reg Harris and was selected for the 1948 Olympics in tandem racing.

After starting in triathlons, he moved to the family’s legacy sport and quickly noticed his bike leg was his strongest. Becoming an elite-licensed racer, he finished seventh in the British national TT championships, although being knocked off by a car led to a back injury which stopped competition between 2014 and 2024. Now back pinning on numbers using his own SpeedPocket – and winning time trials galore in the UK’s south-west – being in the racing environment helps him to understand his customer base and generate ideas.

Pond regards himself as a "fake CEO" and more a hands-on, jack of all trades, doing everything from business direction, budgeting, R&D, product design and social media to fixing machines, using his old bike mechanic nous. Reinvestment in his company has often been preferable to status symbols: when he had the money to consider buying himself a Porsche, a new laser cutter for Nopinz took priority.

Investing in the cutting-edge was worthwhile for their latest skinsuit, the Hypersonic Mk2, building on their original, double-layered (base layer and skinsuit) aero iteration. "We dared to be a bit different with it," he says.

Top speed-suits use a lot of the similar striped fabric on the sleeves, which he dubs 'Super Stripe'. Pond and Nopinz collectively spent four years looking for an aero, textured fabric that would be faster.

A year and a half ago, he found his Eureka material from a company on Italy’s Lake Como and christened it Speedcell. It wasn’t cheap, coming in at roughly £45 a metre at orders of 250 metres minimum, but worth every penny. From a rudimentary aero test, switching from the former material to the new one, the basic prototype showed measurable gains, and they made improvements to the fit. It looks different – sci-fi, even – it feels different, and their testing proved that it saved watts.

An ongoing challenge for Pond is keeping up with UCI regulations. In 2022, the sport’s governing body banned the SpeedPocket at mass events after a consultation with a working group of manufacturers. It was a bitter pill to swallow. "Brands started to cotton on to it and were doing their own versions, but the trouble was, you could hardly see the numbers," he says.

Economic challenges, sustainability, and 'Project 35'

Governing body caprices are just one blast in the face for a business that has faced "one headwind after another" in the last five years.

The vast majority of the cycling industry can relate.

He estimates raw fabric costs have risen "15 to 20" per cent, likely due to the increasing cost of oil and the raw materials used. War has a knock-on effect, with the Russia-Ukraine conflict causing a spike in prices.

Shipping costs have also risen considerably, and Brexit added complications. While Pond produces in the UK, fabrics are bought from European nations or ones outside the continent, bringing pressures associated with import and export.

"Because the industry has been so negative and there’s been so much discounting, you can’t pass it on or win it back," he adds.

From Nopinz’s side, wage inflation and increased National Insurance contributions have added approximately £90,000 to their wage bill across a team of 15, which has been streamlined in recent years.

It all means the customer feels the pinch. A European client will have to pay VAT and additional tariffs as well as possible fuel charges and surcharges from delivery operators, even though Nopinz do customs duties and taxes paid now (i.e. settled by the sender) to try to mitigate nasty surprises. With all the added costs, a would-be buyer might easily abandon their shopping basket and drop off. "That’s been quite hard to navigate," Pond says.

It has become harder to manufacture in the UK and make a profit. Nopinz has been flat in terms of growth in recent years, but making a profit, which he perceives to be rare. "We’d obviously love to see Nopinz go back on that growth trajectory, but we don’t want to do it at the expense of being a sustainable business," he says.

In a crowded market of apparel makers at similar price points, Pond expects they will focus more on the high-end side of the sport and the pinnacle. "I feel that’s where we can differentiate ourselves as a brand," he says.

"We want to have products that people go ‘I’m racing, this is super important, I’ve trained really hard, and I want to make sure I invest in the kit.’ We want them to think Nopinz when it comes to cycling products."

"Being small is good. We’ve got the Speedcell now, and we’re already looking for the next thing – we’ve acknowledged we’ve done that, now someone else is going to do that, and the only way we can stay one step in front is being able to rapidly prototype and produce something," Pond says.

"In a company with a lot more management and structure, it might take two years for a product to be conceived and actually find its way to market. Whereas for us, it can be 10 days if we have to, like something to do with Cavendish."

Ah yes, collaborating with the greatest sprinter in the sport. As office dogs Rodney and Cassandra pad in and out of the HQ boardroom to the whirr of air compressors, Pond locates a pair of surprisingly small white shoes with a blue Nike tick which belonged to the sprinter extraordinaire.

Yes, Nopinz was part of 'Project 35'. Nopinz brand ambassador Alex Dowsett, a fellow aero geek, went to the wind tunnel with Cavendish in the middle of 2024 and called Pond, wanting to fine-tune every possible aero gain in his pursuit of the record.

Turning round prototypes and testing them at Silverstone rapidly, Nopinz worked up toe overshoes ('Hypersonic Tovershoes') and eye-catching textured, shoelace covers. "We tried to simulate the texture of the laces, while also tidying up the aero around the Boa [dial]," he says.

There was also what would become the Hypersonic Mk2 socks, initially called P35, with V-shaped aero chevrons. However, Pond was mindful that, due to UCI equipment rules, anything used for competition has to be on the market. "I said ‘put them on [the website] for £1,000 so nobody buys them’ – and somebody did," he says.

Nopinz also contributed a road race suit for lead-out man Michael Mørkøv and Cavendish. Optimised for hotter conditions using graphene, according to Pond, the Manxman rode it for the sweltering first day across Italy, where he was nearly eliminated in the time cut.

"Unfortunately for us, just not on the stage he won," Pond adds. "But it was super cool to be involved and asked at the eleventh hour, and have someone of Mark’s level and standing. He did ride most of that Tour in our stuff."

Whether it is for road racing’s greatest fast man or the rider looking to win the town sign sprint on the club ride, Pond is constantly thinking about how to get ahead of the competition with his 'everyday aero' apparel. So, what is the future of high-performance clothing in racing?

He imagines fabrics that adjust their own textures to different speeds in the real world. "There are already fabrics that can control how they react electronically, so you can imagine that with a speed suit or something where the texture changes as they go from 30km/h to 50km/h. Optimising itself as you’re riding."

He likens them to people in Tron-style suits, a bit like when Nike did Back to the Future auto-closing shoes. Good luck getting that one past the UCI.

items.title: 'There is certainly no bitterness' – Case against truck driver who struck and killed Davide Rebellin won't continue due to his ill health
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
The hearings into the case of Wolfgang Rieke, the truck driver who struck and killed Davide Rebellin, have concluded with no charges brought.

Two years ago, a first-instance trial concluded with Rieke being sentenced to a four-year jail term after hitting and killing Rebellin in 2022. However, the Venice Court of Appeals ruled last week that Rieke is unfit to participate in an appeal trial, so the case has been dropped, according to the news agency.

Rieke, 66, currently resides in a nursing home after suffering a stroke in 2024, and this summer his lawyers obtained a doctor's report on his psychological and physical ability to participate in the trial. The report concluded that Rieke is mentally unable to stand trial.

"The family acknowledges what happened. There is certainly respect for the judicial decisions and today's. There is certainly no bitterness; there is acknowledgement and respect for his health," said Rebellin's family's lawyer, Davide Picco.

"Justice has certainly worked, given that the Prosecutor's Office transferred the defendant from Germany to Italy. He served several months in prison and then under house arrest. His health condition then led to today's sentence."

Rieke, who had previously pled guilty to a non-fatal hit-and-run and drunk driving, struck and killed Rebellin as he was on a training ride in Montebello Vincentino on November 30, 2022, shortly after he retired from racing. He then fled the scene, leading authorities to launch a multi-country search.

He turned himself in to German police in June 2023 and was later handed a four-year sentence after the judge rejected several initial plea deals. After suffering a stroke two years ago, the case against him will not continue.

"We are satisfied that the judges have accepted our requests, acknowledging Mr. Rieke's current health conditions, which prevent him from consciously participating in the trial," said Rieke's lawyer, Andrea Nardin, according to the Corriere del Veneto.

items.title: Why a 37-year-old Primož Roglič is still a great signing and how more freedom at NSN can unlock his five-time Grand Tour-winning best
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
The further into the off-season it went, the more likely it seemed that five-time Grand Tour winner Primož Roglič's career was going to end before he wanted it to.

It wasn't like most of the big-name moves in modern cycling, which are signposted months in advance, but it did finally bring an answer to the question that Roglič had been answering with "We'll see, ah" and "I don't know yet" ever since July, when Red Bull team boss Ralph Denk confirmed he would be leaving.

The idiosyncrasies that have made him one of the peloton's most popular and compelling riders won't be going anywhere, instead just repackaged in the Swiss team's colours for, as they described it, the "final chapter".

Though it should be noted that Roglič hasn't ruled out a similarly complicated re-up of his time in the sport 12 months from now, more openly putting it down to needing "some time to figure out how to make a chapter in my life where I am peaceful, but the answer is actually simple with the team name: Never Say Never."

Tudor, Pinarello Q36.5, Unibet Rose Rockets, and XDS Astana were among the other speculated landing spots for the Slovenian, but clearly none could muster up the perfect mix of financial resources, a fitting contract, or the desire to bring him in, but NSN have found room for the GC star.

Importantly, it means that instead of a nondescript 68th-place finish at Il Lombardia, 37-year-old Roglič is now in control of where his final chapter as a professional comes to an end, and he certainly won't be looking to go out with a whimper.

"I still believe I have some work to do – in both racing and with myself," he said, when his surprise move to NSN was announced on Wednesday evening. "I have the drive and also the attitude not just to race, but also achieve things."

After his home heroics in Slovenia late in the season, Roglič will start his 12th year in the WorldTour as the reigning European time trial champion, which he wasn't even sure he'd get to wear in a race after he won it: "Maybe I'll only wear it at home. Because we haven't decided yet what I'll do next, but no matter what, I'll wear it."

Off the bike for 10 days and unsure if he would have even taken the start if it wasn't where he lived, Roglič's late-season results should be looked at with the context that what he did was nothing short of miraculous when it came to recovery. This is far from the sort of moves that saw the then Israel-Premier Tech – which was rebranded as NSN a year ago – criticised as something of a "retirement home".

Roglič may be a veteran, but he is still one of the top riders in the world.

Roglič raced 53 times in 2026, with mixed success, but importantly, still with success.

He opened up his campaign with a solid performance at Tirreno-Adriatico, finishing fifth overall and helping teammate Giulio Pellizzari to third on GC behind winner Isaac del Toro, and followed that up with more success in Italy by taking third at Milano-Torino.

From here, things slowed down for the Slovenian, finishing 16th at Iztulia Basque Country, and failing to impress at the Tours de Romandie and Suisse as compatriot Tadej Pogačar dominated the racing to take both titles. Roglič only managed 18th and eighth overall, respectively.

He turned things around at the Slovenian national championships, ramping up his performance with a win in the ITT and fourth in the road race, ahead of his already confirmed major goal of the Vuelta, where he was looking to stand alone at the top of the history books for the most overall titles – which he currently shares alongside Roberto Heras on four.

However, it was soon after, on July 31, that Roglič revealed he had been halted in his plans: "Got hit by a car few days ago…" read a post on his Instagram. "I won't be participating in San Sebastian and in Burgos unfortunately... not the best scenario, but it's life, eh. Now it's all systems go towards La Vuelta; we work and hope things will turn around!"

He did make it to the Vuelta, and while there were no of old – as it was Enric Mas who stepped into the spotlight and claimed red after Pogačar crashed out – when all was said and done in Granada, Roglič could only describe second as feeling "like a victory to me".

Mas rightly took the majority of headlines as he made history for Spain, but there was a more visceral reaction from the press room as second-place Roglič answered his final question in the longer post-race press conferences. It felt like a goodbye to the race where he had enjoyed his most successful moments, with no one in the room, nor he, knowing where he'd end up next as the room filled with applause and matching gratitude from the Slovenian.

The same feelings returned at European Championships and Il Lombardia, where the enigmatic Roglič was none the wiser, still saying, "You never know when is the last one. Like everything in life, it can be a bit emotional," as he conceded that the Italian Monument could be the endpoint.

Into the off-season, Roglič next resurfaced at the Taiwan Cycling Masters, where a KOM challenge south of Taipei saw the Slovenian drop no hints at whether he'd signed a contract – instead, he continued to be cryptic in his comments.

"The people that you collect on the way, or they collect you, that you have around, they help the influence at the end on you," he said in a promotional video for the event.

"I think yes, they left a mark on me, like I said I'm always open to learn, to know more, and the more you know, the more you know that you don't know, so it's a never-ending process."

Well now we do know, as does he, that life in the pro peloton will be continuing, and while those previously ruthless punchy legs perhaps lack the same bite they had five-eight years ago, he has a diesel engine that can still power him up the highest mountains.

In his best results at the Europeans and Vuelta, it's key not to forget that it wasn't against weak fields by any means; at the former, Bruno Armirail, Stefan Küng, and Jakob Söderqvist were among those unable to live with Roglič's time, and at the latter he emerged ahead of Giro runner-up Felix Gall, new teammate Richard Carapaz, and Oscar Onley for his second place on GC.

How he could fit into NSN's plans

Even with Roglič clearly proving his worth as an asset into his late 30s, there still remains the question of how NSN will deploy their new leader and fit him into their schedules after such a late pick-up.

The team's media day is next week, and the thoughts will already be on December and January training camp ahead of the start of the 2027 season on January 1, with rider schedules among the news set to be confirmed in the coming weeks.

With Carapaz, Santiago Buitrago, and Lennert Van Eetvelt, NSN had already been looking to improve their stock as a GC-hunting outfit, having failed to finish in the top 10 of all three Grand Tours in 2026. Their best results were 12th at the Giro, 68th at the Tour, and 15th at the Vuelta, but with those three mentioned above and Roglič, they suddenly have a chance at finishing in the top 10 and potentially higher of all three.

Carapaz has already suggested that it is a return to the Giro where he wants to target an overall placing, and while this would seem to interfere with a potential Slovenian homecoming for Roglič, it's actually the Tour and Vuelta that look like more likely targets.

Sharing the leadership among their new star signings lessens any chance for internal bickering, and also opens the door to Carapaz potentially chasing GC at one Grand Tour and then stages and the mountains classification at another – as he'd been doing successfully for EF in recent years.

NSN's new foray into the GC hierarchy also represents more freedom for a rider like Roglič, who has been bitten by bad luck and crashes several times in the most pressure-filled moments riding for Visma and Red Bull – teams where you to maintain GC success to keep your spot.

Roglič should get the freedom to pick the plan which suits him best and allows him to build up in the ways he knows will work for GT success. NSN will also offer up what Red Bull didn't in his final Vuelta for them this past summer, where a young team lacking in climbing support saw them struggle to front up numbers to muster a major challenge consistently against Mas – even if it likely would have had no effect on the final red jersey standings.

NSN can commit their younger riders Buitrago and Van Eetvelt, and the experience of George Bennett and Nick Schultz to a full-blown Roglič bid, be that at the Tour or Vuelta. And while in an age of Pogačar, Vingegaard, Evenepoel, Seixas, and Del Toro, any entrance into the top-five seems unlikely, this summer proved that anything can happen, even to the big stars, with Pogačar crashing out of the Vuelta and Vingegaard from the Tour, so it's not out of the realms of possibility that he is able to score one final Grand Tour podium, which would be his 10th, or indeed a sixth victory.

In reality, Roglič's goals could become a final stage win at the Tour – to add to the three he already has, 10 years after his first into Serre-Chevalier on stage 17 of the 2017 race – the GC title at the Tour de Suisse, which remains the only major one-week stage race missing from his palmarès from the seven, or indeed that elusive fifth Vuelta title.

Even with Pogačar probably taking the start, living by the words "Never say never" has got Roglič this far, and he'll be hoping his new team's name can carry him to the last hurrah which he deserves. There's a degree of risk in not allowing that European title win on home roads to become the denouement to his great career, but as one Slovenian famously said en route to one of his Vuelta titles: "No risk, no glory."

items.title: Demi Vollering, Eddy Merckx, Paul Seixas among cycling stars set for audience with Pope Leo XIV
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
A host of representatives from the cycling world, including Demi Vollering, Eddy Merckx, and Paul Seixas, will attend an audience with Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican next week.

UCI President David Lappartient described the November 23 event as "an opportunity to strengthen cycling's commitment, as a sport, to promoting peace and intercultural dialogue among peoples."

Past and present Grand Tour champions are among a group of over 100 "distinguished guests" attending, in addition to organisers of all men's and women's Grand Tours and other races, and representatives from various cycling federations.

Vollering, Merckx, and Seixas will be joined by a host of current and former road riders, including Bernard Hinault, Annemiek van Vleuten, Greg LeMond, Elisa Longo Borghini, Francesco Moser, Miguel Indurain, Jeannie Longo, Vincenzo Nibali, Chris Froome, and Mark Cavendish.

Multiple para-cycling world champion Ricardo Ten Argilés, multiple BMX world champion Mariana Pajón, and Ukrainian cyclist Anna Kolyzhuk, who suffered a serious spinal injury in a crash during a race this year, will also attend.

Ahead of the event, Lappartient "highlighted the longstanding historical roots between cycling and the Catholic Church, from races organised by parish communities and cycling teams inspired by Gospel values, to the various meetings with Popes throughout the 20th century and the recent passage of the Giro d’Italia through the Vatican during the 2025 Jubilee."

The event will see Pope Leo XIV take an audience with the riders before the UCI symbolically donates several bicycles to Caritas Rome, a charitable organisation founded by the Episcopal Conference of Italy.

The audience isn't the first time the Pope and the cycling world have come together. In 2025, the Pope blessed the peloton ahead of the final stage of the Giro d'Italia, which started in the Vatican. The stage was dedicated to Pope Francis, who died in April.

Several other Popes have addressed the Giro in the past, including Pope Paul VI in 1964 and Pope John Paul II in 2000. Pope John Paul II also offered his support to the Amore e Vita cycling team in the 1990s and 2000s.

items.title: ‘Who is influencing whom and why?’ – Some of cycling’s biggest backers are spinning a sponsorship spiderweb, but what are the risks?
items.author: Chris Marshall-Bell
items.content:
At Spain’s biggest cycling races next year, one sponsor will be ubiquitous: Lidl.

Plastered across the red leader’s jersey at the men’s and women’s Vuelta a España will be the logo of the German supermarket chain; it’ll also adorn barriers and finish gantries at the Volta a Catalunya and the Itzulia Basque Country; and in each and every race, riders from Lidl-Trek, also emblazoned with the discount chain’s red-yellow-blue coat of arms, will be competing. Given the team’s big-spending habits of recent times, it’s not unfeasible that a Lidl rider will win (many) a Lidl race.

The newly announced sponsorship deals – which are in addition to the Lidl Deutschland Tour, and come three years after Lidl was a major sponsor of the 2023 UCI Road World Championships – are another sign of Lidl’s commitment and interest in mass-participation sport; alongside cycling, it has also significantly invested in football and handball. As the company's customer base and profits reach new heights, so too does its marketing strategy. To promote an active lifestyle to its millions of loyal and new customers, it wants to be seen as the supermarket of choice for athletes and active people.

But does Lidl further extending its tentacles into cycling pose a problem? Is there a risk that too much of the same thing risks threatening the sport? To get to the point: is there a possible conflict of interest issue to address?

Lidl is not the only cycling sponsor with fingers in many pies. MyWhoosh, the virtual cycling platform, has been a long-time sponsor of the world’s best team, UAE Team Emirates-XRG, while simultaneously hosting the UCI Esports World Championships. Similarly, MyWhoosh’s rival, Zwift, is the main sponsor of the Tour de France Femmes, while simultaneously sponsoring the Canyon-Sram team.

Elsewhere, French petrochemical giant TotalEnergies had a team competing in the Tour de France this year, while also being a major partner of the race itself. There are other examples: car brand Škoda, as well as bike component manufacturer Shimano, are also linked with numerous different cycling stakeholders. The list runs and runs.

It’s not a situation unique to cycling: similar multi-partnership arrangements are found in other sports, especially football. The UAE-based airline Emirates, for example, sponsors many of Europe’s biggest clubs, as well as the English FA Cup, the world’s oldest competition. Formula One can point to its own examples.

No evidence – let alone suggestion – has ever been raised of private companies interfering with the integrity of cycling competition. But has cycling reached a point where a select number of brands are spreading their wings uncomfortably wide, leaving open the possibility of them potentially having too much influence over the sport?

Power, success, and a particular image

Sponsors have held sway over cycling teams since bike racing began. Bike teams, after all, are funded by external backers, and they wouldn't exist without their support. Companies telling a team it must select X rider for X race for visibility purposes, as much as for competitive reasons, happened at the outset of bike racing in the 19th century and still happens today.

He and his team would say different, of course, but do you really think Tadej Pogačar has ridden the UAE Tour four times (and is expected to make his fifth appearance in 2027) because he views it as better preparation for his main season goals than, say, the more competitive and less sprint-focused Paris-Nice or Tirreno-Adriatico? It’s unlikely, but his appearance also serves the commercial and promotional interests of the team’s principal backers to have its headline rider in its state-supported home race. The story repeats across the cycling landscape: riders and teams make certain decisions based on the wishes, and sometimes demands, of those who provide the funds. There is nothing inherently wrong with that.

In the first quarter of this century, major international sponsors have shifted their marketing approach, favouring cross-promotion with similar but different partners to reach as wide and as diverse an audience as possible. "Companies realised a long time ago that sponsoring an event is not enough, as some have visibility but others don’t," Professor Jean-Loup Chappelet, one of the world’s leading sports governance academics, told .

"Sponsoring an athlete is better. It goes back a long way; look at Adidas and Nike sponsoring runners. They may sponsor an event as well, and there will be signs around the stadium, like there are on the road in cycling races, but the athlete gives them more visibility. As a result, every sponsor now does both: they have a team of athletes and sponsor events."

Professor Simon Chadwick, who is a leading voice on sport’s geopolitics and economics, concurred. "It’s about power and also projecting a particular image: we are successful, and we associate with successful sports teams and events," he said. "Emirates has the money and power associated with many leading football teams [and the UAE men's cycling team – ed], and they’ve successfully established a narrative that it and its associated clubs are the best of everything."

In a statement to , Lidl said of its various, concurrent relationships: "By partnering with various stakeholders… we aim to support the entire cycling ecosystem. This multi-layered commitment allows us to foster equal opportunities, prominently supporting both men’s and women’s cycling, and to bring the sport closer to a broader audience."

But do these spiderweb-like agreements constitute a headache for sports authorities? "Dense, highly interconnected and deeply embedded relationships exist that are increasingly throwing up contradictions and juxtapositions, meaning we get situations where people are asking questions," Chadwick continued.

"There is no doubt that there is evidence [in other sports] of commercial partners and sponsors seeking to, if not directly intervene to achieve outcomes that they are pursuing, then certainly trying to exert influence."

Evidence of sponsors directly impacting the result of cycling competition is in short supply. What appears more likely, and has been demonstrably proven in a wide range of sports, is that sponsors garner influence at a governmental level. That could mean they earn a seat at the table that decides venue selection for a tournament, or have a word in the ear of a committee member voting on regulation changes.

This is particularly relevant with Lidl: in the ongoing battle to reform professional cycling’s economic model and structural issues, understands that a Lidl employee is part of the UCI’s reform working group, while at the same time Lidl has become a shareholder in the team-led venture, Collective Cycling Group (CCG). That means the German company has a stake in both projects, which could give it influence over decisions that will shape the future of the sport projects.

"You can’t separate these things: governance, hierarchy, big networks, big money, the state, private equity investors," Chadwick added. "It’s become such a dense network that it’s difficult to even begin to unravel it or draw red lines."

The possible issues affecting cycling and the weight a small group of sponsors could have over the sport are worth spelling out – even if, it must be said, they are merely hypothetical for this essay, and there is no evidence that such incidents would eventuate.

If a rider is punished due to an in-race incident, could that team’s sponsor, who also has links to the UCI, use its leverage with the governing body to reduce said rider’s sanction? Could a situation also arise in which an event sponsor lobbies a race organiser to tailor a route towards a rider from a team that they also financially back?

Companies might not even need to wield such clout: those in charge of making decisions might be subconsciously swung towards a particular decision, aware of who is paying for the running of the event or the team. That is essentially how soft power works.

"Lidl operates with a strict, structural separation between its commercial marketing partnerships and sporting operations," a spokesperson for the supermarket said. "As a sponsor of race events, our role is strictly commercial – for example, focused on fan engagement and promoting fresh food.

"We have no involvement in, or influence over, race organisation, sporting regulations, or the decisions made by race juries and the UCI. The sporting integrity of the races is exclusively safeguarded by the independent race organisers and the sport’s governing body.

"When Lidl-Trek competes in a race where Lidl acts as a commercial partner, the team is subject to the exact same sporting rules and competitive conditions as every other team. The race organisers and UCI commissaires ensure an entirely neutral competitive environment. There is no structural or operational overlap between Lidl’s race partnership activation and the Lidl-Trek sporting department."

On the Collective Cycling Group, Lidl said discussions to strengthen cycling's long-term sustainability were ongoing and directed us to the UCI for queries relating to its reform working group.

When asked for a comment on the topic, Škoda said: "Škoda Auto has been a long-standing supporter of cycling and works with a range of partners across the sport. Our partnerships are based on clearly defined commercial and sponsorship agreements and do not extend to sorting decisions or competition outcomes. We respect the respective roles and independence of governing bodies, organisers and teams and conduct our partnerships accordingly."

Additionally, MyWhoosh's Director of E-Sports and Game Operations, Matt Smithson, said: "MyWhoosh is proud to invest across cycling, from our long-standing partnership with UAE Team Emirates-XRG to hosting the UCI Cycling Esports World Championships.

"Each of these is a commercial partnership with clearly defined roles. We have no involvement in team selection, results or sporting decisions in racing. These rest with the UCI, race organisers and the teams themselves. At the UCI Cycling Esports World Championships, the competition rules and results are governed by the UCI. We fully respect the UCI's governance framework and the independence of those who run and officiate the sport.

"Our aim is to grow cycling and make it more accessible to riders everywhere."

What's the UCI's stance on it all?

Speaking more broadly about the perceived conflict of interest, Chadwick added: "This gets to the battle for the soul of sport. What type of governance is there? Are there conflicts of interest? Who is influencing whom and why, and how are they doing that?

"Where is the money coming from, and why is it coming from there? What do people want in return, and who is taking what? That raises the fundamental issue of integrity: who makes decisions about rules? Sports fans need to know that rules are being created fairly and equitably, not on the basis of whoever paid to be a commercial partner. This is where we get issues around rules, bribery and corruption.

"In general, sport has made some progress in the past 20 years towards being better governed, more transparent, fairer and more equitable. But the reality is, despite all the deeds and good words, governance in sport is still really opaque."

In a statement to , the UCI said that it has a "clear governance framework to deal with potential conflicts of interest". It said that the "same brand cannot be the main sponsor of two professional teams at the same time", adding that "the principal partners and paying agent… may act in that capacity for one team only." Members of those teams, "which include its sponsors, may have no link with another UCI WorldTour, a UCI ProTeam [equivalent provisions apply to women’s teams] or the organiser of a UCI WorldTour event that is likely to influence the sporting course of events, or to be perceived as doing so."

There are examples in cycling of a sponsor’s logo being emblazoned on different kits: TotalEnergies on its eponymous team’s and Netcompany-Ineos’s; Red Bull, meanwhile, owns Red Bull-Bora-hansgrohe and is on the sleeve of Tudor Pro Cycling’s jersey. There is no suggestion that either sponsor has sought to favour one team or another in competition.

"When a company chooses to acquire sponsorship rights in several areas of cycling, whether teams, events or the UCI itself, this is a commercial decision based on the visibility each partnership brings to its brand. These rules are designed precisely to strike the right balance: allowing our sport to benefit from this investment while safeguarding the integrity of sporting results."

The responsibility to scrutinise potential problems lies with the UCI Ethics Commission, an independent body that reports its annual findings at each year’s UCI congress.

Biting the hand that feeds you

As the UCI alluded to, mid-sized sports like cycling that are dependent on sponsorship revenue just to survive, let alone thrive, cannot be too picky with where the capital that bankrolls athletes, teams, races and federations is coming from. "One of the core elements in this is the feeling that if we don’t agree terms with them [a partner] then they’ll go somewhere else," Chadwick said.

FOMO – fear of missing out – is real. "Of course it is," Chadwick adds. "But it’s not about a rival team or their riders, but a rival sport. You could sponsor cycling, but you could sponsor golf or tennis instead. Whoever secures that big money will secure a competitive advantage. It’s a common story across many sports."

The consequence of that is that it creates an uneasy situation in which the very questions being mused in this article are asked. "What always talks loudest in sport are not the governing bodies, athletes or fans – it’s the money," Chadwick said. "I remember once being with the sponsorship team of one European governing body, and I asked them on what basis they signed deals with partners. Was it an alignment with values, a particular target market, I asked. ‘No’, they said, ‘there's one criteria only – who pays the most’."

Ultimately, that gives further weight to the sponsors: they know that cycling teams and events are desperate for money, and thus often can’t risk an argument with their paymasters.

Yet perhaps this is all simply a case of making a mountain out of a molehill. Chappelet, who has spent decades researching sports governance, particularly in Olympic circles, suspects it might be. "I do not see a conflict of interest between sponsoring a cyclist and a UCI-sanctioned race organiser, or the UCI itself," he said.

History would agree with Chappelet. As previously noted, there is zero evidence of companies using their leverage to swing a decision towards their supported entity; it bears repeating, none of the hypothetical scenarios mentioned in this article (interfering in disciplinary decisions, venue announcements and course design) have ever been recorded, and nor is there any indication that such companies would look to flex their muscles in this regard.

And there’s another point worth addressing: if a sponsor like Lidl or MyWhoosh cut off its funding to cycling, would the teams or races it sponsors even survive? It’s not a guarantee that a replacement sponsor would step up. Don't bite the hand that feeds you, one might caution.

But as long as a select few sponsors continue writing cheques for riders, teams and the sport’s governing body, the uncomfortable, hard-to-breach matter of undue influence will persist in the background. Even with UCI frameworks that are designed to require transparent governance safeguards – and which, on the face of it, do just that – the reality is that part of cycling’s integrity is dependent on trusting in corporate financiers to act morally and ethically for the benefit of the sport and not for their own commercial interests.

items.title: NSN Cycling Team change bikes for the second time in three seasons as German brand returns to the WorldTour
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
NSN Cycling Team will ride Cube bikes for the 2027 season and beyond after the team struck a deal with the German manufacturer.

Cube will provide the outfit’s World and Development teams with their Litening C:68X Aero and Air road bikes, while the Aerium C:68X will be deployed for time trials. The bikes will roll on Newmen’s Streem range of wheels, with SRAM providing the group sets and other components, while the saddles will be provided by Selle Italia.

Cube will be the team’s third bike partner in as many seasons. Factor provided their rides for a number of seasons when the squad were known as Israel-Premier Tech, but moved on at the end of the 2025 season, with Scott bikes taking their place for the 2026 season.

Now, with the arrival of high-profile GC riders, Primož Roglič and Richard Carapaz for the 2027 season, the team will be hoping for some stability, though it is a return to the familiar for their star sprinter, Biniam Girmay, who rode the brand’s bikes at Wanty-intermarché.

"We are incredibly excited to welcome Cube as our Official Bike Partner," said NSN’s General Manager, Kjell Carlström.

"From our first conversations, it was clear that we share the same vision and ambition. Cube's passion for innovation and commitment to performance make them an ideal partner for our team, as we continue to grow.

"In 2027, we will have more of a General Classification focus and the support from Cube will be fundamental to our success across the entire racing calendar.

"Of course, Biniam Girmay won three Tour de France stages and the green jersey with Cube, so we are looking forward to seeing Bini and his teammates create more memories."

Based in Bavaria, Cube were most recently in the WorldTour in 2025, providing bikes for Intermarché-Wanty, but when that team merged with Lotto for last season, they were forced out in favour of the Flemish squad’s Orbea bikes.

"From our first conversations through to the work already underway, we have been impressed by the team’s professionalism and its clear focus on performance," Cube’s founder and owner, Marcus Pürner, said.

"The team’s ambitions, reflected in its impressive new signings, such as Richard Carapaz and Kasper Asgreen and latest addition Primož Roglič, align closely with our own plans and long-term strategy.

"For us, this partnership also offers a valuable opportunity to work closely with the riders and technical staff, using their feedback and experience to support the continued development of our bikes."

items.title: 'Passion has no age. Class is timeless' – Solution Tech-Nippo-Rali confirm Domenico Pozzovivo will continue racing at the age of 44
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Solution Tech-Nippo-Rali have confirmed that Domenico Pozzovivo will race on with the team next year, the Italian climber continuing in the peloton past his 44th birthday.

"Some riders are part of a team. Others are part of cycling history. Domenico Pozzovivo will continue racing in Solution Tech-Nippo-Rali colours in 2027! Passion has no age. Class is timeless," the team announced on Wednesday.

Pozzovivo, who turns 44 on November 30, has been racing since 2005, with next year marking his 22nd season as a pro. He retired at the end of 2024 as he and his wife Valentina welcomed their first child, Diana, before returning in April on a one-year deal.

Pozzovivo didn't race the Giro d'Italia in 2026 after his team didn't receive an invite, but he told that he's hoping to make a record-breaking 19th appearance at his home Grand Tour next May.

"Now I'm at 18, tied with Wladimiro Panizza, and... yes, I'd like to," he said. "Also because nowadays it's rare for a professional career to last beyond 12-14 years. So it would be a record that, while not unbeatable, could last a long time.

"Competition is the foundation of sport, and yes, I confess that it makes me happy. Finishing ahead of someone less than half my age doubles the satisfaction."

Solution Tech-Nippo-Rali look good for a Giro wildcard invitation next season alongside Polti-VisitiMalta, with Italy's other ProTeam, Bardiani CSF-7 Saber, not eligible for an invitation after missing the top 30 in the UCI rankings.

Pozzovivo would be a leader for the team if they are invited. He finished the season with the second-most UCI points of any rider on the roster, only behind Serbian sprinter Dušan Rajović, and this year achieved a series of eye-catching results at the age of 43.

Highlights of his 2026 season included third-place finishes at the Giro dell'Appennino, GP Beiras a Serra da Estrela, the Czech Tour, and a fourth place at the Mercan'Tour Classic Alpes-Maritimes.

"Between training and races, a million kilometres – actually, even more. At least 1.1 million. And I still haven’t stopped," he told .

"Training isn't a big deal for me, and I enjoy cycling. My performance, considering my age, is decent. So I turn the tables: why shouldn't I? Besides, I'm naturally drawn to challenging myself and my limits. That's the main thing."

Pozzovivo said that he had to negotiate with his wife to continue racing. He's balanced family life with time on the bike, while he has also completed his third degree (studies in nutrition sciences have followed previous degrees in business economics and sports science), with a fourth possibly upcoming.

"It was a fairly long 'negotiation', so to speak. When I stopped, at the end of 2024, one of the reasons was to be as close as possible to my daughter, who was about to be born," he said.

"But I started again because I realised that things could be reconciled, given that cycling is still important but no longer comes first. I'm trying to put it all together, and I think I can do it.

"If you love studying, and I do, it's right to continue doing so because staying up-to-date is essential – keeping up with the latest discoveries in practice. Specifically, I've delved deeper into nutrition sciences because it's something that, in endurance sports, now affects performance by 50%.

"Next year I'd like to take the state exam to become a nutritional biologist. To answer your question... Maybe, but I don't rule out the possibility that I might be interested in a Master's degree."

Now, however, Pozzovivo will turn his focus to training for 2027 and that possible return to the Giro d'Italia, where he's finished in the top 10 on seven occasions. Will it be his final season on the bike?

"We'll see. It's not a given," he concluded.

items.title: Tour de Romandie saved as Primeo Energie steps in as sponsor for both women’s and men’s races
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
After a lack of funds was cited as a major contributing factor in the cancellation of the 2026 Tour de Romandie Féminin, the race will return in 2027 with Primeo Energie stepping up to sponsor both women’s and men’s races.

The Swiss electricity company have sponsored the races’ mountains classification jerseys since 2022, the first year of the women’s race, but will now be the main sponsor of both events for the next two editions.

Even before the 2026 race, the organisation was in trouble, hoping to address a 10% budget shortfall by attracting Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates). But a week after he won four of the five stages and the general classification, organisers, Chassot Concept SA, announced the postponement of the 2026 women’s race.

"This postponement also aims to preserve the Foundation's financial stability and, ultimately, to guarantee the quality and long-term viability of the event," organisers said at the time.

Now, with Primeo Energie on board, not only is the men’s race secure, but the women’s event will return in 2027, with the three-day stage race due to start on September 10th.

"We have seen just how deeply the Tour de Romandie is rooted in the hearts of the people of French-speaking Switzerland," Primeo Energie’s CEO, Cédric Christmann, said. "We are strengthening our presence in a region where we intend to continue our growth.

"Supporting the women’s race is also particularly important to me; women’s cycling deserves more attention - much like the energy sector, especially regarding technical roles and leadership positions."

Unlike the men’s race, which began in 1947, the women’s race has a short history, starting as recently as 2022. Then Ashleigh Moolman-Pasio beat Annemiek van Vleuten on the mountain stage to the ski centre at Thyon 2000, going on to take the only WorldTour general classification success of her career.

Held in 2025, the most recent edition was won by home rider Elise Chabby (FDJ-SUEZ). The race also witnessed the emergence of Paula Blasi, who won the opening day mountain time trial, collecting her first WorldTour victory. However, the race was undermined when five teams were excluded from the race before the start.

While details of the women’s race are yet to be released, organisers chose the sponsorship announcement to publish details of the 80th edition of the men’s race, which will start with its traditional prologue on Tuesday, April 27 and feature a number of circuit-based stages.

"We have opted for loop-style stages, with each one taking place almost entirely within a single canton," said organiser Richard Chassot.

"This allows the public to see the riders multiple times in a festive atmosphere. This format also addresses safety requirements, which are becoming increasingly complex and costly."

  • Prologue - Yverdon-les-Bains (4.7km)
  • Stage 1 - Romont - Romont (170.1km)
  • Stage 2 - La Chaux-de-Fonds - La Chauxde-Fonds (176.2km)
  • Stage 3 - Vully-les-Lacs - Vully-les-Lacs, ITT (14.6km)
  • Stage 4 - Sierre - Sierre (141.7km)
  • Stage 5 - Moutier - Canton du Jura (Distance not yet known)

items.title: Tour Colombia returns for 2027 after two-year break with multiple WorldTour teams expected to race
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
The early-season Tour Colombia returns to the calendar in 2027, with the race's fifth edition set to run January 26-31.

The race was founded in 2018 as the Colombia Oro y Paz and has run editions in 2019, 2020, and 2024. It was cancelled in both 2025 and 2026 due to financial difficulties.

It's back next season, however, with its return announced in September. Last week, the race was unveiled in a presentation in Medellín attended by former winners Egan Bernal and Sergio Higuita, as well as a host of other Colombian cycling stars, including Santiago Buitrago, Fernando Gaviria, Nairo Quintana, and Rigoberto Urán.

This week, the route for the 2.1-ranked race was unveiled, and the first teams confirmed to take part were also announced.

Colombian outlet has revealed that WorldTour teams Netcompany Ineos and EF Education-EasyPost will be taking part. It's likely, then, that Bernal, Harold Tejada, Iván Sosa, and Juan Felipe Rodríguez will be racing.

US squad Modern Adventure Pro Cycling will also be on the start line, as will Colombian Continental squads NU Colombia (the team of 2024 champion Rodrigo Contreras), Medellín-EPM (featuring Óscar Sevilla), GW Sportfitness, Sistecrédito, and Orgullo Paisa.

reports that NSN, Movistar, and Caja Rural-Seguros RGA could also be at the start.

The most recent edition in 2024 saw Contreras take overall victory by six seconds from Richard Carapaz, then racing for EF, as Mark Cavendish, Nairo Quintana, and Alexey Lutsenko also took part.

Those who are racing will face a six-day run from Medellín to the final summit finish atop the Alto de Palmas. The 904.2km route will be confined to the Antioquia region, with the toughest stages coming in the last two days of the race, including a penultimate stage finish atop the climb to the Alto la Unión.

items.title: 'A bold new visual era' for the maglia rosa as MAAP strikes deal to produce Giro d'Italia leaders' jerseys
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Australian cycling kit company MAAP is promising an eye-catching revamp of the Giro d’Italia leaders’ jerseys after agreeing a multi-year partnership with organisers RCS to provide apparel across their range of races.

As well as the men’s and women's Giro d'Italia, the agreement will also see the brand providing jerseys for RCS’s other Italian stage races, including Tirreno Adriatico and the Giro Next Gen.

There will also be jerseys for one-day events like Milan-San Remo, Strade Bianche, and Il Lombardia, though they won’t be worn in the race or awarded to winners.

MAAP, which was only founded in 2014, first entered the European pro peloton in 2024, producing a striking design for women’s Continental team Lifeplus-Wahoo, before going further with the current purple Jayco-AlUla and Liv-AlUla Jayco team kits.

To continue in that eye-catching vein, MAAP is promising "a bold new visual era for the most beautiful Grand Tours".

understands the new pink jersey design for men’s and women’s Giro d'Italia will be a significant departure from the old produced by Castelli, though it will not be revealed until sometime in the New Year.

"The partnership seeks to bridge the deep traditions of European racing with contemporary culture through performance and design," MAAP’s press release states.

"Bringing a progressive perspective to some of cycling's most iconic symbols, MAAP will honour the heritage of these events while challenging conventions through a new approach to technical apparel and visual expression."

It’s been a remarkable rise for MAAP, which was founded in 2014 in the Australian city of Melbourne and has always produced kit that looks a little different to that of other companies. Their first team partnership was for Australian Continental team State of the Matter, before partnering with Trinity Racing in 2019.

"From the start, we set out to make the world’s best cycling apparel, paired with a design language that lights up the sport," said company founder Jarrad Smith.

"The Giro d’Italia has shaped the performance and aesthetic of cycling for more than a century, and it holds a special place in my heart. It’s the race that got me into road cycling. Stepping into that living history, and helping progress the Maglia Rosa and some of cycling’s most storied races, is a defining milestone and a privilege. It’s also a statement of our respect for the sport’s history and our passion for where it can go."

CEO and General Manager of RCS Sports and Events Paolo Bellino said: "MAAP is a young and ambitious company, it stands out for its use of technologically advanced materials and its strong design identity. We are confident that the new jerseys, which will be unveiled soon, will generate great interest among all cycling fans, and particularly among younger generations.

"We hope that this partnership with MAAP will lead us into a new era, one that is even more modern and innovative, while continuing to respect the great tradition of the Giro d’Italia and our races."

The deal comes hot on the heels of Castelli’s partnership and sponsorship agreement with ASO to provide leaders’ jerseys for the Tour de France, Tour de France Femmes and their other races, including both men’s and women’s Vuelta a España, though it is thought the sponsorship element of MAAP’s deal is absent.

items.title: 24 teams come together to form Collective Cycling Group, the latest venture aiming to 'unlock the value' of pro cycling
items.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
items.content:
Following the collapse of the One Cycling project that aimed to reform professional cycling into a more lucrative business model, a new group has officially made its presence known with similar aims but stronger support. The Collective Cycling Group (CCG) issued a press release on Wednesday announcing the new movement.

It was stated that 24 teams from the men’s and women’s WorldTour and ProTeam ranks have already signed up, and that there are ongoing discussions with additional teams. Several teams have shared news of the announcement, indicating that they are part of the movement, but not all have.

The CCG aims to "develop and market selected commercial rights and activities to strengthen the economic model of professional cycling", according to the announcement.

It also wants to "unlock the value potential of professional cycling, elevate the product to better serve a global fan base, and address the need for a more sustainable economic model in professional road cycling and the broadening of its global reach".

The company is registered in the UK and is essentially the same entity as One Cycling, with government files showing the name was changed to Collective Cycling Group on June 2, 2026.

Soon after, ownership of the project changed hands, with Visma-Lease a Bike team boss Richard Plugge standing down both as a 'director' and 'a person with significant control', and replaced in both cases by Oliver Ciesla, a sports marketing executive who previously worked in motorsport.

"This broad and inclusive initiative by so many teams represents a significant milestone in the long and proud history of the sport," Ciesla said.

"Teams carry much of the sporting and financial risk in professional cycling, while many of the sport’s commercial opportunities remain fragmented. The UCI reform process creates a first opportunity to address these challenges together.

"Through a closer cooperation with organisers, the UCI and other stakeholders, teams can create products that none could offer alone, enhancing the experience of fans worldwide, increasing the sport’s visibility, and contributing to a sustainable economic model."

It was not stated in the launch announcement which 24 teams have signed up to form the Collective Cycling Group.

Some teams have since publicly shared the announcement, indicating they are on board. Those teams include EF Education, which has men’s and women’s WorldTour squads, Canyon-SRAM, and Pinarello-Q36.5.

Given Richard Plugge’s prominent role in One Cycling and the push for reform more generally, it can reasonably be assumed that Visma-Lease a Bike are part of the project.

According to , 13 of the 18 men’s WorldTour teams have signed up. The five absentees were said to be UAE Team Emirates-XRG, Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, Netcompany-Ineos, Jayco-AlUla, and Groupama-FDJ United.

Revamping pro cycling's business model has been a decades-long ambition for many of the stakeholders of a sport

Tour de France owners Amaury Sport Organisation (ASO) are one of the few to be profiting off the sport.

The UCI's formation of the ProTour (now WorldTour) under Hein Verbruggen could be considered to be one of the first attempts at modernizing pro cycling, although the effort was met with extreme resistance from the ASO.

The WorldTour promised to bring more stability to teams, with three-year guaranteed entry into the biggest races, but the sponsorship model of professional cycling remains on shaky ground.

Teams with billionaire backers and generous budgets dominate the sport, while smaller outfits such as TotalEnergies have had to fight for their lives after sponsors pull out.

Even One Cycling wasn't the first try at a new model: In 2011, the Rothschild financial group were backers of what was then called a 'breakaway league' - the World Series Cycling (WSC), with 14 teams on board.

The Velon group came in 2014, with a more modest ambition to add on-board footage and real-time rider stats to their marketing campaigns. How teams really benefited from being a part of Velon is less concrete, and mainly helps with fan engagement and commercialization.

How the CCG will differ from the previous attempts remain to be seen.

How the new CCG project will be received by the UCI should become more clear after the WorldTour seminar, which runs from December 9-10, 2026.

The topics included calendar and participation, the economic model, fan engagement, safety and integrity.

Some of the ideas floated in the document include shortening Grand Tours to 16 days, budget caps, and joint broadcast rights.
