items.title: 'Now time to get serious' – Tadej Pogačar wraps up off-season of travelling, running, and fellow pro's wedding, as 2027 preparations set to begin
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Tadej Pogačar has announced that it's "now time to get serious" as he calls an end to his off-season ahead of ramping up preparations for a racing return in 2027.

The Slovenian former world champion was forced to end his 2026 campaign prematurely after crashing out of the Vuelta a España. After recovering from his injuries, he has spent recent weeks travelling and enjoying time away from serious training and racing.

Pogačar's latest stop came in Ireland at the weekend, where he and his partner Urška Žigart attended sometime training partner Eddie Dunbar's wedding in Killarney. He wasn't riding his road bike while in Ireland, but was spotted by several locals riding a mountain bike and going for a run in the woods.

"Now time to get serious. But before that, spent some nice moments around the world," Pogačar wrote in an Instagram post on Tuesday.

"Sometimes cycling gives you more than just wins. Thank you Eddie Dunbar and Niamh O'Keeffe for having us there on your special weekend (yes, Irish weddings are long)! It was sound."

In a change from two wheels, running seems to have been a theme of Pogačar's off-season, with a video as part of his post showing him on another run, by the coast.

Next up for Pogačar will be a return to serious training as he prepares for 2027, with a meetup with his UAE Team Emirates-XRG team for a training camp in south east Spain next month.

His early-season schedule isn't yet known, but he is set for a return to the UAE Tour in February, a race he's won on three occasions in the past. Last month, he offered a suggestion of his main goals for 2027 – the Tour de France, Vuelta a España, and the Road World Championships – but the full outline is set to be confirmed in mid-December at the training camp.

items.title: Rapha Pro Team Shadow winter glove review: A good addition to the Shadow range but perhaps not the best value
items.author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
items.content:
58 grams per pair - Medium

Yes

Rapha resurrected its Shadow range of foul-weather and winter clothing last year, and has expanded it coming into this winter season.

Gloves were included in that expansion, and the brand has released the Pro Team Shadow Winter gloves, which sit alongside the Shadow gloves in the winter lineup.

The Pro Team Shadow gloves are, in the brand’s words, ‘engineered for hard training in cold and damp conditions’.

These are thinner gloves that are designed to offer good dexterity and protection from the elements. They are also, given their ‘Pro Team’ name, designed with more purposeful riding in mind, where hands will stay warmer when you are generating that little bit more heat, but of course, you can use them for anything.

My glove testing for winter is well underway for our best winter cycling gloves guide. Whilst there’s still some warmth left in the sun's rays in my part of the world (UK), I’ve sought out some freezing conditions to put them through their paces.

If you are shopping for a thinner pair of light/mid weight gloves this winter, this review should give you the inside track on some of Rapha's new Shadow products.

These are thinner gloves designed with more purposeful riding in mind; they are also well suited to slightly milder temperatures or riders who don't want or need too much of a bulky glove.

Rapha says it has used its ‘Shadow technology’ in the makeup, meaning the gloves feature its Shadow membrane and a DWR coating. The Shadow membrane is an in-house offering from Rapha.

Rapha lists a temperature range for these gloves of 0-7C / 32-45F. If you are going hard in the cold, that might be ok. It depends on the rider, but if you are looking at these gloves for general fall riding in cooler conditions, I would recommend wearing something warmer below about 5C / 41F.

There’s Japanese OCTA thermal insulation in parts of the inside, and what looks like the same grid-shaped fleece that features on the Pro Team Bibtights and Pro Team Shadow Winter Jacket; it’s good stuff, similar (if not the same as Polartec Power Grid) and has always kept me comfortable.

The gloves pull on, extending a few centimetres up the wrist; I've worn them over and under long-sleeve base layers, arm warmers, jacket sleeves. The length is good.

The index finger is touchscreen compatible, which is just as well as the gloves do need a fair pull to get on, especially if you are slightly damp. Rapha recommends sizing up if you are in between sizes.

Two fingers, the top of the thumb and the palm also have a series of grippy dots applied, and grip is good on brake hoods and bar tape.

The entire thumb is covered in a soft nose wipe material, which is great; it's nice to have in the cold, and I'm glad Rapha has included it.

There are also some pretty specific care instructions on the Rapha website. I assume to look after the PFAS-free DWR, Rapha says to wash in a laundry bag at 30 degrees Celsius, and to rinse twice after washing. You can also tumble dry to reactivate the DWR. If the waterproofing was amazing, I’d be more motivated, but I’m not sure I’m going to have motivation to rinse these things twice after every wash.

Branding is minimal, with a small Rapha wordmark on the outside of each wrist and the recognisable Rapha dashes on the little finger. Black and Laurel (a kind of light grey) colours are available.

I’ve worn these gloves across a wide range of autumn temperatures, from the low teens to five degrees above freezing and in the rain. One of the first things I learnt about them is that they are not a pair of gloves to choose for anything more than light rain.

Within 40 minutes, I had soaked hands wearing them in medium rain on a gravel ride, my first outing with them. They resisted water for a little while, but were quickly overcome and got pretty waterlogged. My lower overall off-road speed did lead to my hands getting uncomfortable. I felt the thumb-wipe panel was probably one of the main key weak points regarding water ingress.

For intermittent rain or light showers, you may be ok, especially if you are going hard, but they won’t stand up to much water, so bear this in mind.

In the cold, going hard, they perform very nicely. I wore them on my local chaingang in 5ºC, riding hard, and they kept my hands comfortable without getting sweaty, ditto for various sets of uphill intervals, which is pretty much what they say they will do on the tin.

A feature I really like is the nose wipe panel, which covers most of the thumb. It’s really soft, and just helps when you need to wipe your nose in the cold. It’s probably my favourite feature and has been well executed.

Putting the gloves on and off isn't the easiest; for instance, taking them off for uphill intervals and then putting them back on for steadier riding is ok, but that tighter cuff makes it a little trickier.

When you are just trying to crack on, little things like that can be annoying in the winter cold. Breathability is decent, though, so perhaps more riders will just leave them on, and generally I have too.

For general riding, in cooler conditions, they work well too; they are thin enough to provide very good control and dexterity, and do a decent job of keeping your hands warm and comfortable. As an autumn option, or a thinner glove for more intense riding, they do their job well.

These are fairly pricey gloves at $120 / £80 / €95. They are well executed, look good, and do their job well. However, the rain protection is minimal. Switching to a neoprene offering in rain may be the way to go, but that does mean buying another pair of gloves.

These are a competitor to the popular Castelli Perfetto RoS 2 glove; those gloves are designed for a similar purpose using Gore-Tex Lab's Windstopper and a soft internal fleece and retail for £85 / $95. Does that Castelli Gore-Tex Windstopper label just carry a little more weight?

Despite being a similar weight, there perhaps isn't quite the same amount of insulation as the Q36.5 Termico gloves, but those gloves don't have a nose wipe panel or touchscreen compatibility like these ones do.

These are a solid pair of gloves, seemingly good quality and well made, and they do their primary function very well, but you can achieve the same performance for less money.

A good pair of lightweight gloves from Rapha that do what they say on the tin. They provide good warmth, dexterity and wind-blocking properties in a neat package.

They look good and fit well, but aren't going to handle too much rain, so don't expect them to.

The Pro Team Shadow gloves will carry you through Autumn and Spring and down to close to freezing if you are riding hard and generating heat and don't want the bulk of a bigger glove.

Testing scorecard and notes

A good design that does what it says on the tin. Some protection in the wet, but not very much. Nice subtle styling.

Not great, wet hands within 60 minutes in the rain. Although these gloves aren't designed to deal with lots of rain.

Good across a wide range of temperatures. These aren't heavy winter gloves, but offer enough warmth when riding harder in some quite cold conditions.

Comfortable with a great thumb nose wipe panel. Id maybe just like the wrist to be a touch stretchier.

A little on the pricey side, par for the couse for a Rapha Pro Team product. Good gloves, but you can achieve the same for less without doubt.

items.title: 'A special place in my heart' – Alexey Lutsenko returns home to XDS-Astana for a new role after racing retirement
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Recently-retired Alexey Lutsenko is making a return to his former team, XDS-Astana, for 2027, taking on a role as head coach after calling time on his 14-year professional racing career.

The 34-year-old spent all but the final two years of his career with the Kazakhstani team and retired in October as one of the most successful Kazakhstani riders of all time.

Along the way, he took 43 pro victories, including stages of the Tour de France and Vuelta a España as well as overall triumphs at the Tour of Oman (twice), the Arctic Race of Norway, the Tour of Turkey, and Giro d'Abruzzo.

Having spent the final two seasons of his career racing with NSN, Lutsenko is now heading back 'home' with XDS-Astana as part of the team's sports performance group.

"The Astana project has a special place in my heart. Almost my entire professional career took place here," Lutsenko said.

"This is where I achieved nearly all my major results and found a sporting family. That is why returning to the project, albeit in a new capacity, and continuing my career in sport beyond racing brings me nothing but positive emotions."

Lutsenko will work under returning General Manager Yana Seel as Alexandr Vinokourov reportedly takes a step back to focus on the sporting side of the team. He'll join another former pro, XDS-Astana Performance Engineer Alex Dowsett, among the sports performance group.

The team also counts some recognisable names among their directeur sportif group, including ex-pros Dmitry Fofonov, Peter Kennaugh, Dario Cataldo, and Alexandr Vinokourov Jr.

"I know that the transition from being a rider to becoming a team coach will not be easy, and that I will need time both to gain experience and to adapt to this new role. However, I believe in myself, my abilities and my knowledge, and I am confident that with hard work everything will work out," Lutsenko said.

"I know that I have a wealth of sporting experience behind me, which I would like to share both with the project’s young riders and with my former teammates and colleagues from the peloton. I hope I can make a valuable contribution to the team as we work towards achieving our shared goals in 2027."

On the road, XDS-Astana will welcome Anthony Turgis from TotalEnergies for 2027, while a pair of climbers – Lidl-Trek's Andrea Bagioli and Kern Pharma's Urko Berrade – are other notable additions.

Notable names heading out the door include Sergio Higuita to Caja Rural-Seguros RGA, Davide Ballerini to Pinarello-Q36.5, Harold Tejada and Clément Champoussin both to Netcompany Ineos.

items.title: Wout van Aert seeking damages in bizarre case of Belgian municipal employee who illegally accessed personal information of 30 pro cyclists
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Wout van Aert is among several riders caught up in a data protection court case in Belgium after a municipal employee accessed the personal data of a host of riders.

The public prosecutor of the Belgian city of Mons has requested a sentence of 120 hours of community service for the defendant after he accessed the personal data of various people, including election officials and 30 bike riders, reports the news agency.

A host of leading racers have been caught up in the case, with the defendant having accessed the data of Van Aert, Remco Evenepoel, Mathieu van der Poel, Greg Van Avermaet, and others between January and September 2023.

"Initially, it was for electoral purposes. Then it became an unhealthy curiosity. I wanted to know where the cyclists lived," the defendant admitted, according to .

The investigation began after suspicious activity was discovered on the defendant's computer on the municipal system in La Louvière.

The municipality suspended his computer access before taking disciplinary action and later dismissing him.

As part of the case against the man, Van Aert and his wife, Sarah De Bie, joined as civil parties.

The pair are seeking a symbolic €400 in damages in the case, with their lawyer emphasising "the need to protect their privacy and that of their children", according to

Any damages would then be donated to charity.

items.title: Just seven weeks after launching, the new season-opening Canary Islands race has been called off
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
The inaugural edition of the Vuelta Ciclista a Canarias, set to be staged in January 2027, has been cancelled, the race's organisers announced on Monday.

The race, to be held on the Canary Islands 1,000km off the Spanish mainland, was set to run for four days between January 14-17 on the islands of Tenerife and Gran Canaria, with ambitions to expand to six days in the future.

However, the organisers have said that the race will be postponed "in order to ensure all the organisational, logistical, and safety conditions that an event of this scale requires". The debut edition will now take place in January 2028.

"Since receiving confirmation of the dates in the last week of September, we have been working intensively and at a demanding pace on all preparations: designing routes, creating professional race itineraries, and holding meetings with state security forces, the Government Delegation, and the municipal authorities of the start and finish locations in both Gran Canaria and Tenerife," read a statement from the organisers.

"Throughout this process, we have benefited from the trust and collaboration of public institutions, which have shown their support for the project. However, despite the significant work completed and the progress made, we believe that the current timeline does not yet provide all the necessary guarantees to ensure the optimal execution of a competition of this nature."

Showcasing the 'eternal spring'

The stage race was announced at the end of September, and in October, race organiser Noelia Pérez told that the motivation for staging the race was to offer an alternative to early-season racing in more remote destinations and to show that warm-weather riding is available in Europe year-round.

"Here we train in short sleeves and shorts 365 days of the year, and we wanted to show that. You have to see that to believe that," she said.

"Plus there's a lot of racing in Australia and the Middle East at that time of year, but this is for those who've stayed in Europe who say 'Ooh, let's go and find some warm weather in the Canary Islands'. Because if they're on the rollers training indoors on the mainland because of the cold, we've got what we call 'the eternal spring' here.

"Being the first race of the year also shows people what they can do in the Canary Islands as well."

However, riders will now have to wait another year to take on the first-ever edition of the Vuelta Ciclista Canarias, which was set to run as a 2.1 UCI-ranked race.

"Out of a sense of responsibility and commitment to the institutions, participants, teams, and fans, we have decided to reschedule the event for January 2028," the statement continued.

"Throughout 2027, we will continue working to finalise every detail, ensuring that the Vuelta Ciclista a Canarias becomes a resounding success for Gran Canaria, Tenerife, the Canary Islands as a whole, and – most importantly – for cycling and sport in general.

"This decision reflects our commitment to carrying out this project with the rigour, professionalism, and ambition that the Canary Islands deserve."

items.title: 'Our ambition is to build the fastest kit in the world' – Rapha returns to the WorldTour as racing kit supplier to Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Rapha is making a return to the WorldTour peloton as the official performance partner to the Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe team.

The British company has been absent from the top-level peloton this season after its deal to supply the EF Education men's and women's teams expired at the end of the 2025 season.

Rapha and Red Bull have entered into a "multi-year agreement", with the company replacing Specialized as the team's kit manufacturer.

In announcing the deal, Rapha hailed Red Bull's willingness to disrupt the sports it enters, including cycling, "bringing an unsurpassed level of global engagement, scale and energy".

Meanwhile Ralph Denk, Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe CEO, said that Rapha has proven "it can change the face of cycling".

Rapha, which was founded in 2004, entered the pro peloton with Team Sky between 2013 and 2016, and went on to outfit Canyon-SRAM from 2015 to 2022, and then EF from 2019 to 2025.

It is currently the supplier for USA Cycling across various discilines, with Brandon McNulty winning the road race world title in Rapha in September, but this marks the brand's return to a trade team partnership.

"Returning to the WorldTour is a hugely exciting moment in Rapha’s story. We are back in the pro peloton with one of the sport’s most ambitious teams, backing riders winning at the very highest level," said Christina Lindquist, Rapha's global marketing director.

'An engineering challenge'

The agreement was not billed as a simple supply relationship, but rather a partnership that will see new products be developed, with "a shared ambition to build the fastest race kit in the world".

The companies are approaching kit design "as an engineering challenge", as Rapha shares resources and expertise from its in-house team, while drawing on expertise from within the team, with Head of Engineering Dan Bigham namechecked as a key point of contact.

"Working with a WorldTour team of this calibre is an extraordinary privilege and a huge technical opportunity. We get to work with Dan Bigham as Head of Engineering, clothe the best in the world, riders like Remco [Evenepoel] and [Florian] Lipowitz, and put Rapha back where we believe we belong: at the pointy end," said Joel Natale, Rapha's chief product officer.

"Our ambition is to build the fastest kit in the world. That means treating it as an engineering problem and rethinking how cycling apparel is developed, so that every detail becomes an opportunity to improve performance.

"We are going to push the boundaries of what apparel can make possible for riders at the highest level, with innovations that will ultimately benefit every Rapha rider."

'Rapha was a true gamechanger'

Denk, meanwhile, believes the partnership can go beyond performance and help to increase cycling's ability to reach bigger audiences.

Rapha certainly shook up the cycling kit market when it came onto the scene in the 2000s and went on to produce some of the most striking kits in the pro peloton with EF and Canyon-SRAM, though the company has more recently faced challenging financial circumstances.

"As a team, we have a clear mission: to make cycling bigger and inspire new audiences to embrace our sport. Rapha is an important partner in bringing this vision to life," Denk said.

"The brand has proven in the past that it can change the face of cycling. Rapha was a true gamechanger, bringing lifestyle into the sport and reaching entirely new audiences. Now, we want to take the next step together and inspire even more people to fall in love with cycling.

"Rapha and Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe share a desire to do things differently and find new ways to move the sport forward," he added. "This partnership brings our performance ambitions to life while giving us a platform to transform how people see and experience the sport together on the world’s most visible proving ground."

We'll have to wait a little longer to get a glimpse of the team's new kits for 2027, with the new season's collection set to be unveiled in December.

items.content:
There's no question that at just 20 years of age, Paul Seixas looks one of the most likely contenders to inherit the position which Tadej Pogačar currently occupies as cycling's number one rider. But even with his warranted confidence as the youngest Monument winner since 1944, the French star can admit that winning the Tour de France remains a dream out of reach for the moment.

Seixas was in Japan as one of the headline stars for the Tour de France criteriums in Singapore and Saitama, the latter race seeing him with a last-lap move to win ahead of Brandon McNulty. Speaking to a small group of anglophone media, including , in Japan, Seixas gave some early insight into his goals for the 2027 season, with the Tour not even down as a definite target for the moment, as he weighs his options for the race he most wants to win: the World Championships road race.

"I said the World Championships because it's home for my grandparents. It's the parents of my father, and it's from their side that I start cycling, so it's really important for me," said Seixas.

"And it's a unique opportunity for me because I think maybe it's my only chance to do a World Championship there, and it would be really important also for the French.

"I would say it's maybe one of my main goals next year, and maybe my main goal. But I guess we'll see how it goes. I will talk about it with my coach to see what is the best way to approach this World Championship. Even though I want to do a Grand Tour, which will be of course one of my main goals of the year, we'll have to see how we can make it."

While his future beyond the 2027 remains unknown, Seixas has enjoyed this period of "vacation" where he hasn't had to think about where he'll race from 2028 onwards. When he returns home from Japan, though, the thinking will immediately turn to contract discussions, and planning out his upcoming race calendar.

"The [media] are talking about it, but I said I'm still on vacation, actually, and I didn't think a lot about this," he said.

"Every year we make the plan around December. We will talk about a lot with my sport directors and the head of the the coaches of the team. But for the moment, I didn't think a lot. I think there's a few possibilities around the Worlds, and of course I will do a Grand Tour, but for the moment I don't know what one I would do honestly."

'For the moment, I'm not able to win the Tour'

What's certain is that France's first yellow jersey in the men's race since Bernard Hinault in 1981 and a rainbow jersey are the long-term goals for Seixas, but he certainly sees the latter as the more attainable.

Realistic about the improvements he would have to make to be on the level of a Pogačar over three weeks, Seixas shows more signs of his maturity, but at the rate he improved in 2026, there's no ruling him out of taking another massive leap in ability in 2027.

"My biggest long term goal is to win the Tour de France, but I say it always like it's a dream for the moment because I'm not able to [win it]. But it is my biggest dream, so it's my biggest long term goal," he said.

"It's a dream, and for the moment, with what I showed this year, I'm not able to win the Tour. But we cannot know what can happen next, so I will try to make some progress, and then I will see what happens. But I think it's more of a very long-term goal, and I need to be at the start of the Tour de France to dream to win it. Anything can happen, but for the moment, I don't think about this."

Even without knowing his schedule yet, he did point to a potential Italian opening to his 2027 season when thinking about what some of his short-term goals might be.

"We cannot really talk about short term goal because it's like in March, so it's difficult. But I know that I will do – I'm pretty sure of it, I don't know for the moment because I didn't do the plan – but I think that I will do Strade Bianche then Tirreno," said Seixas.

"Then this is a short term goal because I will, one month before this race, not be racing, so it's a short not long-term goal."

With wins at La Flèche Wallonne, Itzulia Basque Country, and Il Lombardia among his impressive successes as a teenager, Seixas, now 20, in his third year as a WorldTour pro will be hoping for similar jumps in form. Just like his chances of winning the Tour, Seixas knows he is not yet the best rider in the world, but by the way he speaks, it's clear that is what he is in search of.

"I mean, I will have expectations, but I don't know if I can still make progress like last year and this year," he said, after bursting through to the upper echelons of the sport in unprecedented quick time.

"I guess we'll see, but I will work even harder to try to make a step again. Then it depends how it goes, but I'm already at a good level. Of course, I'm not the best in the world, but I can compete at the highest level. So I guess I just I will just work and see if I'm making progress during the winter, and then after that I will maybe see where I can put my expectations."

items.title: Drones clear a hurdle for use in anti-doping control transport
items.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
items.content:
Drones have been floated as delivery methods for companies such as McDonald's, Amazon, and DoorDash, and may now be on the horizon for use in anti-doping efforts in sports.

The International Testing Agency, the independent organisation responsible for most of professional cycling's anti-doping controls, announced a proof-of-concept study that supports drones as a feasible option for transporting athletes' samples over short distances to laboratories for analysis.

The peer-reviewed study, published in September, was performed in Doha, Qatar, in 2022 as part of the ITA's "Integrity in Flight" project that previously evaluated long-range sample transport over 1,000km in Alaska.

In the Doha study, researchers collected urine, blood and dried blood spot (DBS) samples from over 20 volunteers, then performed standard Athlete Biological Passport testing, including steroid profiles, blood values and other metabolic factors either without transport or after drone flights of 5km and 20km before being tested.

The researchers found no significant differences in the results, and no changes during drone flight that would change a sample from negative to positive or vice versa.

The drone used in the study, the RigiTech Eiger, is capable of flying almost 120 km/h with a max flight distance of 100km, but can only carry 3kg, which limits the number of samples that can be transported in each flight.

Drone delivery could help solve logistical problems in prompt delivery of anti-doping controls in congested city centres, such as during the Olympic Games, or from remote areas where travel by road takes much longer than flying directly. For example, the Sallanches stage of next year's Tour de France is just 60km as the crow flies to WADA's Lausanne laboratory, but is 130km by car.

"Innovation is essential to addressing practical challenges in anti-doping, but it must always be underpinned by robust science and the highest standards of sample integrity and chain of custody," said Benjamin Cohen, Director General of the ITA.

"Through this research, we are assessing whether drone technology can become a reliable additional option for transporting samples over long distances or across difficult terrain. The findings may also have applications beyond anti-doping, particularly in helping remote communities access laboratory and medical services more quickly and efficiently."

WADA has requirements for the prompt delivery of doping control samples, with a maximum of 60 hours if samples are kept on ice or 27 hours if the average sample temperature is 15°C.

While those times are rather generous, WADA Senior Director, Science and Medicine, Prof. Olivier Rabin supported the idea of drone deliveries when reacting to the Alaskan study.

"Transporting samples to WADA-accredited laboratories for analysis can be an expensive and logistically difficult process for Anti-Doping Organisations to ensure full integrity of the samples during the transportation phase, especially from remote or difficult-to-access areas to the laboratories.

"Modern technologies have the potential to successfully alleviate some of the challenges while not compromising quality.

"They must, of course, be robustly tested to ensure they are fully reliable and fit-for-purpose in the anti-doping context. WADA commends the ITA and its partners for seeking to innovate in this way."

items.title: 'An important signal for women's cycling' – FDJ United-Suez welcome major new title sponsor as TotalEnergies takes big step into women’s WorldTour
items.author: Matilda Price
items.content:
FDJ United-Suez will become TotalEnergies-FDJ United in 2027 and beyond after striking a significant five-year deal to bring the French energy company into the women's peloton for the first time.

The deal, which team manager Stephen Delcourt tells only came together in the last few weeks and months, marks an important milestone moment in the history of the French team, which has grown from a small squad in 2006 to the most successful team of 2026, with rapid growth particularly over the last five years.

"We are incredibly proud today. One of France’s greatest business success stories is joining our team: TotalEnergies who, alongside FDJ UNITED, will support our national and international ambitions for the next five years," Delcourt said in a press release.

"This new chapter in the story of our squad allows us to establish ourselves at the very top of the global sport, and also to continue to deliver on the two goals of our raison d’être: shining a spotlight on women’s sports and inspiring young people to see sport as a means to personal and professional fulfillment."

Current title sponsors Suez will depart as a result of the new partnership, with Delcourt adding: "I would also like to express my deepest gratitude to SUEZ Group, who has helped us achieve so much since 2022." FDJ United, who have been title sponsor of the team since 2017, will continue as second naming partner.

'It was really, really fast'

Changing title sponsors was not necessarily on the cards for 2027, Delcourt explained, speaking to earlier on Monday, but the opportunity to partner with TotalEnergies arose over the summer.

"It was after the Tour de France, but it was more after the season," he said. "We know that TotalEnergies were really interested to invest in women's sport and women's cycling, because they are already a partner of ASO for the Tour de France and Paris-Roubaix Femmes, so we have the same network and there are events where we're together.

"So I had a special conversation with the CEO and after that it was really natural that we speak about how we can work together, but in fact it was really, really fast – if you called me one month ago, I was not able to speak about that, it was not a clear project. But when somebody wants the same thing and has the same values then you want to grow together."

Signing a deal for five years is particularly significant, as many deals in the pro peloton – even headline sponsor deals – are only signed according to the WorldTour license cycle, but Delcourt has secured the longest deal in his team's history to underwrite their future.

"To sign for five years, especially in this moment of the worldwide economy, it's really comfortable for us and it's an important signal for women's cycling. Two leading French companies with really strong international footprints and goals, to invest in women's cycling, I think is really, really important for our discipline.

"2025 and 2026 were incredible seasons, so after that, after these last six years, to have the signal to sign with a big company like TotalEnergies for five years, for us, wow, it's more than a win. Or maybe it's win number 34."

TotalEnergies retreat from men's peloton and invest in women's peloton

TotalEnergies is ending its title sponsorship of Jean-René Bernaudeau's long-running men's team at the end of this year, having begun its sponsorship in 2016 with Direct Energie, a company that was acquired in 2018 by the energy giant then known simply as Total.

TotalEnergies is also a non-title sponsor of the Netcompany Ineos team, appearing on British team's jersey since the middle of 2025, with reports in the past 18 months that a larger sponsorship package was being explored. It is unclear how this latest news leaves that particular relationship – has contacted TotalEnergies for clarity.

In any case, it is significant that a long-term sponsor of the men's peloton is now focusing on women's racing.

"After more than 10 years of supporting the TotalEnergies men’s team, we are continuing our commitment to cycling by embracing women’s cycling," said Patrick Pouyanné, chairman and CEO of TotalEnergies.

"TotalEnergies is pleased to promote the visibility and growth of women’s cycling at the world’s highest level. We are proud to support the ambitions of these champions and to share the values we cherish: team spirit, performance minded and the determination to move forward together. This partnership also reflects our commitment to giving women their rightful place, both in sport and within our company."

For Delcourt, this is a result of the growing popularity and excitement around women's racing, which is often praised as more thrilling than it's men's counterpart.

"For me, it's really important that everybody understands that women's cycling now offer a different kind of spectacle and performance. Last week I was listening to a cycling podcast on French radio, and they said that it's really, really interesting to follow women's cycling because we never know what can happen. There is always a show."

Delcourt also hopes that the arrival of yet another high-profile sponsor into women's cycling can bring visibility and benefit to the sport at all levels, not just for his team.

"I really hope this announcement can benefit to all the women's cycling areas – for the other WorldTeams but also for Continental teams, junior teams, for all the federations – that now companies can invest in women's cycling. I really hope that when other brands see that TotalEnergies want to invest, [they think] 'Oh, maybe we need to look at women's cycling' and they will invest, because I don't want to grow if the others don't grow. We need all of the ecosystem to grow together."

What growth in the new TotalEnergies era will look like for the FDJ team is not yet decided, not least because the planning has only just begun, but Delcourt was clear that it won't be about immediately going out and buying new flashy riders.

"First, short term, we need to invest and structure the company because we are a big team on the sport level, but we need to grow also as a company," he said.

"We want to structure more on the administrative and financial side of the team and the team departments to improve also as an employer and to be a comfortable place for my staff. A new performance coach will arrive, a new CFO will arrive. We want to help also all my logistics managers to optimise, to be efficient. So for me, that will be my hobby for the first quarter of 2027, to start the next generation project."

"We started [that process] before TotalEnergies because we started also a cyclo-cross team and the name of the cyclo-cross team is Specialized TMRW – there is the word 'tomorrow' and that is an important one. The team is a tomorrow project, because for us to be good now is good, but we want also to be good tomorrow.

"Now with a five-year partnership with TotalEnergies, we have the resources to work in an efficient way and to create something. I don't know now exactly what we want to do about the formation in general, but we really want to invest in the next generation to be good at the present and the future. I'm really excited about this part."

TotalEnergies-FDJ United will unveil their new jersey and branding in December.

items.title: 'I've never stopped believing in what I can achieve' – Four-time Olympic medalist Chloé Dygert circles back to US-based TWENTY28 squad to reignite career ahead of LA Games
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
Multi-discipline world and Olympic champion Chloé Dygert will return to racing for the next two seasons with US-based Virginia's Blue Ridge TWENTY28, the UCI Continental team where she began her career as an emerging world talent in 2015.

The Indiana native competed on the junior development squad for then-branded TWENTY16, which also had a roster that included Kristin Armstrong, a three-time Olympic gold medalist and Dygert's coach at the time. Dygert had her breakout season at the age of 18 when she swept junior titles in the time trial and road race at both US Road Nationals and World Championships, the latter thrusting her onto the global stage in Richmond, Virginia.

Nicola Cranmer, who founded the TWENTY28 programme in 2005, confirmed Dygert had been signed a two-year contract, bringing her full circle to the programme for a firm target on the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games.

“Chloé has a God-given gift, and I've never doubted her ability to achieve extraordinary things. Her talent and commitment combined with the right environment makes all the difference. Our goal is to provide the infrastructure to perform at her very best,” said Cranmer.

"Together, we’ve learned what’s required to compete at the highest level and will work closely with the US National Team to prepare for LA 2028. Chloé’s best chapters are still ahead of her and we’re excited she’s back home.”

Despite multiple surgeries, extensive rehabilitation, and further setbacks, Dygert demonstrated extraordinary resilience, adding two more World Championship titles and three Olympic medals to her remarkable palmarès, including Team Pursuit gold in Paris in 2024.

"Coming home to TWENTY28 means more to me than I can really put into words. I've never stopped believing in what I can achieve," Dygert said in a team statement.

"Nicola [Cranmer] believed in me from the beginning and has never stopped. I’m grateful to her and the team for welcoming me home and supporting my health, recovery, and goals. I want to give myself every chance to discover what I’m capable of, and I can’t think of a better place than where it all began."

During her time with the TWENTY16 and TWENTY20 programmes, Dygert earned 10 World Championship titles across road and track, an Olympic silver medal in the Team Pursuit at the 2016 Rio Games, and numerous international victories. Those years account for 10 of her 12 world titles to date and established the foundation for a career defined by success at the highest level of the sport.

"I don't know what the next two years will bring, but I know I want to give myself every possible chance to find out. And I can't think of a better place to do that than where it all began," Dygert added.

The team will collaborate with USA Cycling on her road and track preparation, shaping a race and training program around her health, performance, and ambitions for Los Angeles. Dygert's return reinforces TWENTY28's longstanding commitment to developing young talent and supporting athletes across multiple Olympiads, the team name changing every four years to reflect the next cycle.

In the coming weeks, the full roster for the 2028 Virginia's Blue Ridge TWENTY28 team will be announced, returning for a 12th season at the Continental level for women.

items.title: 'I think I've learned so much from him on the Grand Tour aspect' – Remco Evenepoel enthusiastic about Grand Tour progress under new coach Tim Heemskerk
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
As he looks ahead to his second season with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, Remco Evenepoel has taken a look back at 2026 and his switch to a new coach.

Evenepoel's longtime coach, Dan Lorang, departed for Lidl-Trek during the spring while his team brought on board Tim Heemskerk from Visma-Lease a Bike. The switch seemed to pay dividends for the Belgian as he scored a career-best second-place finish at the Tour de France, as well as securing World Championships time trial domination and European Championships gold.

Speaking on last week, Evenepoel discussed the coaching switch and the benefits Hemskirk's coaching has given him.

"That was a pretty tough change, I must say. Obviously, that was a big, big change. The first 10 days were pretty difficult to adjust to his way of thinking and for him to adjust to mine and get to know each other in such a short time for such a big event. It went smoothly, but it's always strange in the beginning.

"I think I've learned so much from him on the Grand Tour aspect. I think I'm also making him learn things about one-day races. In Grand Tours, he's done so many good things and now second with me. It shows he knows what he's doing with the Grand Tours, for sure."

Hemskirk increased strictness around certain parts of Evenepoel's training regime to help him reach another level.

"It's been really strict on the training. Like if you do 15 minutes more, he wasn't really caring. But in terms of intervals, he was spot on – not like 10 watts above because it could kill me because I was really slowly building. It was really like trusting the process," Evenepoel said.

"He's really committed, and he's really passionate about what he's doing. It also drives me because if I feel somebody so motivated with me, it also brings up the motivation inside of myself."

Now the goal for the 26-year-old is to make the jump to the next level in races, which would mean competing with five-time Tadej Pogačar on a more even and consistent basis.

Evenepoel used an example of his speciality, time trialling, to illustrate his point.

"What I'm doing in the one-day TTs, I would really like to bring that into the Grand Tour TTs as well in terms of performance. I feel like in one-day TTs, if I can bring them to Grand Tours as well, I'd gain even more," he said.

"We need to find this kind of shape and baseline of power, and then on a super day it would be even better. What is now very good, I'd like to have as my standard. I think that's something over winter we'll have to see how and when and why we can, or maybe can't, do that."

The main goal of Evenepoel's 2027 season is likely to be a return to the Tour, where he should go up against Pogačar as well as Jonas Vingegaard and Paul Seixas. With 71 time trial kilometres featuring in France, it's no surprise that Evenepoel spies opportunity in France next July.

"I think it's already a big step forward compared to last year's, and the year before was even less," he said.

"The first TT is not technical at all, long and straight, so that's really something that should suit me. Then the one in Toulouse is pretty flat until the bottom of a climb, one little punchy climb I think we did it in the 2025 Tour. I think it's a three-minute climb, so that's something that suits me as well," he said of the pair of time trials.

"We need to make a strategy to arrive at the two TTs as fresh as possible, drop the hammer big time and then see what the result will bring in terms of the GC gaps.

"It shows that I can take a nice little advantage before going into the Alps, which would help and can give some comfort in mind. Some days in the Tour last year, I had a certain level, especially on the stage I won and the TT. I think those were my best days in the Tour, so that should become my standard."

items.title: Angry confrontation as final corner wipeout sees both leaders lose out on victory in Belgium's biggest beach race – Video
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
The 2026 road season may be behind us, but there's still racing drama to be had elsewhere as the winter rolls in.

Of course, the first port of call is cyclo-cross, which dominates attention in Belgium and the Netherlands up to the Cyclo-cross World Championships in Oostende in January. But there's also excitement elsewhere, as the De Panne Beach Endurance race – one of the biggest beach racing events of the winter – showed on Sunday.

Road pro Timothy Dupont (Tarteletto-Isorex) seemed all set to beat 1,000 other riders and take the big win right at the end of the race's 30th edition. That was until French racer Samuel Leroux crashed into him just metres from the finish.

Within sight of the line, Leroux's tyres slid out as the pair rounded the final bend of the race, which was off the sand and on a brick surface. Dupont had the lead on the outside, but Leroux was taking a tighter line on the inside and went sliding into his rival, taking them both out.

The collision spelt disaster for the pair, with neither able to remount quickly enough to complete the final metres and win. Instead, another Belgian, Jasper Dejaegher, picked his way through the mess to nip through and take an unexpected victory.

Behind him, the recriminations started as Dupont stood up to confront Leroux, forcefully jabbing his competitor in the chest in a brief coming together that only compounded the pair's embarrassment.

According to , race winner Dejaegher wasn't overly proud of the outcome, either, the 25-year-old saying, "I don't want to win like this."

Dupont later placed the blame on Leroux for the spill. "It's a shame that I have to lose in such a way," he said, according to .

"Leroux simply didn’t brake. With sand on the tyres, something like that leads to disaster. He crashed and took my rear wheel with him. A pity, because I was safe through the corner. This defeat, therefore, feels very bitter, because I had plenty of time left."

items.title: Lidl-Trek unveils new cyclo-cross team but Thibau Nys stays with father’s squad
items.author: Lyne Lamoureux
items.content:
Lidl-Trek team announced that it will field a cyclo-cross team with multi-discipline riders Blanka Vas and Fleur Moors as the first big names. The CX team will be managed by directeur sportif Tom De Kort, who joins from De Ceuster Bouwkranen Cycling Team, starting November 22.

Revealed on social media, the Lidl-Trek CX team will make “its debut next weekend.”

In a surprise move announced in September, 25-year-old Vas revealed she would leave SD Worx-Protime for Lidl-Trek, with the switch taking effect on October 1 rather than the usual January 1. The formation of Lidl-Trek’s new cyclo-cross team could explain the unusual timing. At the beginning of 2026, the Hungarian went on to finish fourth at the UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships in Hulst.

In the 2025-26 CX season, Moors raced for cross legend Sven Nys’ team Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions. After her fourth-place finish in the U23 race in Hulst, she claimed a runner-up finish on the road in Wevelgem for In Flanders Fields.

One name that is missing from the list is European champion Thibau Nys. The 24-year-old Belgian races for the German WorldTour team on the road, but not in cyclo-cross, where he lines up for his father’s squad. He has a contract with each team until 2028.

Father Sven told Wielerflits that Thibau was asked but did not want to switch to a new team.

"They have asked him that question before", Sven told . "But we have a contract and we are going to stick to it.”

"Crossing for Lidl-Trek is not an issue for the time being,” Thibau Nys added. "For the time being, everything will continue as it goes. That is going very well, everything goes in a good relationship. I hope it can stay that way. At the moment there is no reason for changes, because the contracts are still running. And I'm happy about that."

Also racing for the elder Nys squad is Lucinda Brand. In order to stay with the man that she credited for helping her rediscover her love of racing, the world champion switched on the road to Canyon-SRAM Scalable Capital for two years after spending nearly half of her 18 years in the pro peloton with Lidl-Trek. Brand also re-signed for two years with the CX squad.

items.title: Paula Blasi back on the bike eight days after fracturing elbow during grocery run
items.author: Lyne Lamoureux
items.content:
Paula Blasi’s off-season faced an unexpected hurdle when she fractured her elbow while doing a grocery run on her bike. Though the injury didn’t stop her from training on her rollers and at the gym, she was back on the bike outside eight days after the crash, as she shared on her YouTube channel.

“I went for a ride in the morning. Everything was fine. And then in the afternoon, I went for a grocery shop, down the street. So I took my bike, just with a stupid thing on the floor I didn't see. Just crashed flew over the bike and laid on fully on my left arm. So all the weight went there and my elbows are strong but not that much,” she said, showing the fracture X-ray in the video.

Her video showed her progress with recovery, and the 23-year-old rider was back training two hours on rollers, 72 hours later. She did adjust her setup to keep her upper body straight.

After four days, Blasi said that she was happy with the progress, as she was seeing “more mobility” and was “already starting to be able to put both hands on the handlebars.”

For Blasi, a silver lining was the fact that it forced her to change her approach to her weight training: “I always like to go way too hard and put way too much weight. With my coach, we're trying to take this moment to really focus on the technique.”

A follow-up X-ray eight days post-injury showed that “the bone is not collapsing, nothing is moved and everything is healing good”, and Blasi was back training on the bike outside, while taking precautions.

“I just tried to go for a couple of hours ride which felt good, not amazing because still my arm is a bit like not super secure and obviously I'm missing a lot of strength now. But I took it super easy in the downhills and tried to find my legs a bit in the climbs.”

Balsi is not giving up on taking on a cyclo-cross race in December.

“Probably the next video will be my next cyclocross race, which I'm not going to announce yet just because I'm not sure I will be able to race because we need to see how the arm goes and obviously I will not race if I feel I’m not secure on my bike.”

Blasting through the Women's WorldTour peloton this year, Blasi won the Vuelta Femenina and Amstel Gold Race in just her first full season as a pro this year and also finished fifth overall on debut at the Tour de France Femmes. She then went on to sign with the Spanish squad Movistar after breaking her contract with UAE Team L’IMAD.

items.title: X2O Trofee Hamme-Zogge: Thibau Nys powers to victory in four-way battle at tactical fast Bollekescross
items.author: Lyne Lamoureux
items.content:
In a thrilling final lap, Thibau Nys took his third victory in three races this cyclo-cross season at the Bollekescross at Hamme-Zogge on Sunday.

The second round of the X2O Trofee series came down to a four-way battle on the 10th lap after the Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions rider waited to take the front before the single-track section, and though he made a few small mistakes, the European champion was able to hold off rivals to the end.

Behind, Michael Vanthourenhout (Pauwels Sauzen-Altez Industriebouw) and Joran Wyseure (Crelan-Corendon) battled for Nys’ wheel, while Niels Vandeputte (Alpecin-Premier Tech) stayed at the back of the quartet.

Nys led onto the finishing straight and initially sat up to celebrate, but after a quick look over his shoulder, he did a few more pedal strokes before he finally raised his arms in victory. Vandeputte came charging from behind to snatch second place, edging out Vanthourenhout, while Wyseure finished fourth.

“It was a really tough one. I don't know since when was the last time since I suffered so much but it makes it even sweeter to take the victory.

The second round of the time-based series returned to Hamme-Zogge, revisiting the fast, explosive and technical course for the first time in nearly 20 years. The layout led to group racing, with riders battling for position and looking to find the fastest lines through the narrow single-track sections.

Though Mees Hendrikx (Bomba Join) took the holeshot, it was Gerben Kuypers (Pauwels Sauzen-Altez Industriebouw) who led the single-file 38-rider field onto the opening single-track of the course. Then, several racers took a lap at the front, just showing what they had, trying to force mistakes further down the bunch. Nys stayed around the fifth to eighth spot, learning the course, and waiting.

Halfway through the race, things heated up as Joris Nieuwenhuis (Heizomat-Cube) applied pressure at the front, accelerating out of every corner and splitting the group as riders were starting to dive-bomb on turns and protecting their positions with elbows out.

With three laps to go, Wyseure made his move, putting a lot of power down to reduce the lead group to 13 riders as riders battled to stay second wheel. One lap later, with Wyseure still at the front of the now nine-rider group, Nys had started to move up. Before the end of the penultimate lap, Vanthourenhout, seemingly fine after crashing out on Saturday’s Superprestige Merksplas race, took the front before the narrow section leading to the finishing straight.

On the bell lap, Wyseure first tried to squeeze through on the outside of the single-track, and then managed to take the front after the first time through the materiaal zone, pushing Vanthourenhout to second spot. But Nys was charging up, taking advantage of Vanthourenhout sliding out on a corner to slot in behind Wyseure. 

Nys dabbed after the planks, and was then forced to close a few bike lengths to Wyseure, finally passing him before the stairs.  Wyseure and Vanthourenhout continued to fight for Nys’ wheel as the lead group, down to four riders with Vandeputte at the back, sped towards the finish line.

items.title: X2O Trofee Hamme-Zogge: 'It's getting harder and harder to win' - But Lucinda Brand Brand takes win number seven
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
The Baloise-Het Poetsburea Lions rider appeared to struggle on some parts of the course, but was able to out-drag Italian champion Sara Casasola (Crelan-Corendon) on the long finish straight, taking the win and maintaining her lead in the X2O Trofee series.

With Casasola second, Amandine Fouquenet (Pauwels Sauzen- Altezt Industriebouw) crossed the line in third place, 10 seconds behind the winner.

After her mid-week crash Brand had appeared to struggle on one of the run-ups, stopping before remounting for the descent, as well as appearing slower than her rivals on the technical whoop section. However, it was there she made her race winning move, gapping Casasola, and though the Italian came back to her wheel, the Dutchwoman had too much power in the final.

The result was a repeat of the X2O Trofee’s first round at the Koppenbergcross, so the one-two in the series remains the same.

"Every victory is very nice to have and it’s getting harder and harder to win,” said Brand. “As you can see in the races, the pack is much more together than last year, so this victory is very nice. She’s really strong,” Brand said of Casasola. “Of course last season she already was strong, and she had to battle with her health, but already on the road I saw this summer if she stays healthy she’s going to be a hard competitor."

For 2027, the Hamme round of the X2O Trofee did not cover the Flandriencross route of recent years, instead returning to the Bollekescross route of more than 20 years ago. Though there wasn’t too much mud, it was not as dry and fast as Saturday’s Superprestige, which Brand also won.

It was Brand who led early in the race, though, the World Champion getting clear the moment the race headed off the long tarmac start, passing habitual fast-starter Fouquenet, with Denise Betsema (De Ceuster Bouwkranen) on her wheel. The three women finished the first of the seven laps with a two-second lead on a chasing group, but the race soon came back together.

Despite the compressed group, Brand continued to lead for most of the second lap, though Fouquenet put her nose on the wind late on, but the race remained mostly together and only on the third lap did anyone gain any kind of lead. This time it was Betsema attacking on one of the steep banks and taking seven seconds onto lap four, though Brand was having none of it, bridging then passing her Dutch compatriot.

After winning the Niel Superprestige on Wednesday, Manon Bakker (Velosport Veluwe) soon reached the leaders and the trio began to establish an advantage. Behind them, though, the ever combative Casasola recovered from a poor start and set about chasing them down, crossing the line only three seconds behind, catching them shortly afterwards.

Casasola led onto the penultimate lap, but Fouquenet began eating into the leading quartet’s advantage, joining them before the lap’s half-way point. She tried her luck on the final circuit too, but Brand was able to match her pace, and the group came back together. However, over the whoop section of the course, Brand powered on, gapping all but the Italian, before opening the taps after the run-up and dropping the Italian as the final section approached.

items.title: 'Expectations are sky-high’ - Annemiek van Vleuten warns Demi Vollering that her successful 2026 could be hard to match
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Demi Vollering had a stunning year in 2026, winning the Tour de France Femmes for the second time, and taking maiden titles at both the UCI Road World Championships and the Giro d’Italia Women, while riding for an FDJ United-SUEZ team built around her.

There were a host of other successes too, but Annemiek van Vleuten, the woman Vollering succeeded as the World’s best female cyclist, has cautioned that such success could be hard to match.

For years Van Vleuten was the preeminent cyclist in the women’s peloton, herself winning Classics, World titles, Olympic gold and all three Grand Tours. In 2022, when she won the inaugural edition of the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift riding for Movistar, Vollering was second, the race somewhat of a handing over of the baton to the next generation, with the younger woman winning the race the following year.

Since then, Vollering has become ever more prolific, bagging a total of 71 wins, with 16 of those coming in 2026 alone. She began her victorious streak in mid-February, winning two stages and the GC at the Volta Femenina de la Comunitat Valenciana, the first race of her season, and finished in early October with the UEC European road race title.

But, according to Van Vleuten, who has her own fair share of success, following such a brilliant season could be very difficult.

"She has had an incredible year. I wouldn't call her a revelation, but then again, kind of," Van Vleuten said at the De Laatste Etappe cycling gala in Utrecht, reported . "She has become a much more complete rider and now radiates a bit more calmness. She has become more mature, I would say.

"The expectations are sky-high. From herself, especially, but also from the outside world, it will also be very difficult for Demi Vollering to match this season and find new goals. The World Championships are, in any case, already tailor-made for her."

The courses for both the Tour de France Femmes and the Giro d’Italia are already published, and both suit Vollering’s skills to the ground.

And if Vollering proved anything this year, it’s that victory at the Giro d’Italia Women and the Tour de France Femmes in the same season, a feat Van Vleuten completed in 2022, is entirely possible, especially now the Giro has moved from early July to early June, providing more time to recover and refocus. Now, after the Vuelta Femenina changed from its early May spot on the calendar to after the men’s Vuelta a España, winning all three in a single season is also possible, the 2027 race will take place in early October.

"Maybe she can try to win all three Grand Tours. The Vuelta will also be positioned differently in the season schedule now, so I am very curious to see what she will do," Van Vleuten finished.

Vollering is not only hugely talented, but also incredibly ambitious, and though her race programme is yet to be made public, a historic assault on all three women’s Grand Tours and a successful defence of her rainbow jersey is very much possible.
